Sharp singularity asymptotics for discrete random matrices

Xuanang Hu Address: Shandong University, Jinan, China. Email address: xuananghu7@gmail.com , Zeyan Song Address: Shandong University, Jinan, 250100, China. Email address: zeyansong8@gmail.com and Xinglong Wu Address: Shandong University, Jinan, China. Email address: wuxinglong3@gmail.com
Abstract.

We resolve the Rademacher singularity conjecture: an n×nn\times n matrix with independent uniform {−1,1}\{-1,1\} entries is singular with probability (2+o⁡(1))​n2​2−n(2+o(1))n^{2}2^{-n}. More generally, for an n×nn\times n matrix MnM_{n} with independent entries uniform on a fixed set S⊂ℝS\subset\mathbb{R} of cardinality q≥2q\geq 2, we prove

ℙ⁡(sn​(Mn)≤z/n)≤C​z+an​(S)+C′​n1+ε​q−n\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(s_{n}(M_{n})\leq z/\sqrt{n}\right)\leq Cz+a_{n}(S)+C^{\prime}n^{1+\varepsilon}q^{-n}

for all n≥1n\geq 1, z≥0z\geq 0, and ε>0\varepsilon>0, with C=C⁡(S)C=C(S) and C′=C′​(S,ε)C^{\prime}=C^{\prime}(S,\varepsilon). Here sns_{n} denotes the least singular value, and an​(S)a_{n}(S) sums the probabilities of zero rows or columns and equal or opposite pairs of rows or columns. The proof combines inversion of randomness with Fourier averaging at scales within a polynomial factor of qnq^{n}.

Key words and phrases: 
Random matrices, smallest singular value, singularity probability, finite support, Littlewood–Offord theory
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
60B20, 60C05, 15B52

1. Introduction

Let BnB_{n} be an n×nn\times n random matrix whose entries are independent and uniform on {−1,1}\{-1,1\}. A natural question is to determine the probability that BnB_{n} is singular. Two equal or opposite rows, or two equal or opposite columns, force singularity. The probability of their union is (2+o⁡(1))​n2​2−n(2+o(1))n^{2}2^{-n}, and it has long been conjectured that these elementary dependencies give the full asymptotic:

ℙ⁡(Bn​ is singular)=(2+o⁡(1))​n2​2−n.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(B_{n}\text{ is singular}\right)=(2+o(1))n^{2}2^{-n}.

See Conjecture 1.1 in [30], Conjecture 2.2 in [33], and equation (4.1) in [26].

Komlós [13] proved that the singularity probability tends to zero, and Kahn, Komlós and Szemerédi [11] obtained the first exponential upper bound. Subsequent work introduced several methods that now play a central role in the subject. Tao and Vu [28] developed inverse Littlewood–Offord theory, relating large concentration probabilities to additive structure. Sharper structural descriptions were obtained in [31, 19]; see [18] for a survey of the theory and its applications. A geometric approach to invertibility through small ball estimates and the decomposition of the unit sphere into compressible and incompressible vectors was developed by Rudelson [24] and by Rudelson and Vershynin [21]. The exponential bound for singularity was improved by Tao and Vu [29, 30] and Bourgain, Vu and Wood [1]. Tikhomirov [32] introduced inversion of randomness and proved the optimal exponential estimate

ℙ⁡(Bn​ is singular)=(12+on​(1))n.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(B_{n}\text{ is singular}\right)=\left(\frac{1}{2}+o_{n}(1)\right)^{n}.

Jain, Sah and Sawhney [10] determined the singularity asymptotic for every fixed nonconstant finitely supported real distribution that is not uniform on its support. They showed that zero rows or columns and equal or opposite pairs of rows or columns give the leading contribution. Their work also gives the optimal exponential rate for uniform finite support laws. For sparse Bernoulli matrices, Litvak and Tikhomirov [15] and Huang [9] obtained sharp results in regimes where the Bernoulli parameter may depend on nn. Song [27] treated highly biased discrete distributions. The precise singularity asymptotic for fixed uniform finite support laws, including the Rademacher law, remained open.

We establish this asymptotic for every uniform finite support law, with an error smaller than the main term by a polynomial factor. Our result also controls the lower tail of the least singular value. Let ξ\xi be uniform on a fixed finite set S⊂ℝS\subset\mathbb{R} with q=|S|≥2q=|S|\geq 2, and let Mn=Mn​(ξ)M_{n}=M_{n}(\xi) have independent entries distributed as ξ\xi. The entries are not normalized. Write

sn​(Mn)=infx∈𝕊n−1∥Mn​x∥2.\displaystyle s_{n}(M_{n})=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\lVert M_{n}x\rVert_{2}.

For an independent copy ξ′\xi^{\prime} of ξ\xi, define

an​(S)=2​n​ℙ​(ξ=0)n+n⁡(n−1)​(q−n+ℙ​(ξ=−ξ′)n).\displaystyle a_{n}(S)=2n\mathbb{P}\left(\xi=0\right)^{n}+n(n-1)\left(q^{-n}+\mathbb{P}\left(\xi=-\xi^{\prime}\right)^{n}\right). (1.1)

This is the sum of the probabilities of the elementary dependencies described above, since ℙ⁡(ξ=ξ′)=q−1\mathbb{P}\left(\xi=\xi^{\prime}\right)=q^{-1}. In particular, an​(S)=ΘS​(n2​q−n)a_{n}(S)=\Theta_{S}(n^{2}q^{-n}).

Theorem 1.1.

Let S⊂ℝS\subset\mathbb{R} be a fixed set of q≥2q\geq 2 points. There is a constant C1.1>0C_{\ref{thm:main}}>0 depending only on SS such that for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 there is a constant C1.1′>0C^{\prime}_{\ref{thm:main}}>0 depending only on S,εS,\varepsilon for which

ℙ⁡(sn​(Mn)≤z/n)≤C1.1​z+an​(S)+C1.1′​n1+ε​q−n\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(s_{n}(M_{n})\leq z/\sqrt{n}\right)\leq C_{\ref{thm:main}}z+a_{n}(S)+C^{\prime}_{\ref{thm:main}}n^{1+\varepsilon}q^{-n} (1.2)

for every n≥1n\geq 1 and z≥0z\geq 0.

Taking z=0z=0 gives the following consequence.

Corollary 1.2.

For every fixed 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1,

ℙ⁡(Mn​ is singular)=an​(S)+OS,ε​(n1+ε​q−n)=(1+o⁡(1))​an​(S).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(M_{n}\text{ is singular}\right)=a_{n}(S)+O_{S,\varepsilon}(n^{1+\varepsilon}q^{-n})=(1+o(1))a_{n}(S).

In particular, for independent uniform {−1,1}\{-1,1\} entries,

ℙ⁡(Bn​ is singular)=(2+on​(1))​n2​2−n.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(B_{n}\text{ is singular}\right)=(2+o_{n}(1))n^{2}2^{-n}.

For independent uniform {0,1}\{0,1\} entries, the corresponding formula is

ℙ⁡(Mn​ is singular)=(1+on​(1))​n2​2−n.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(M_{n}\text{ is singular}\right)=(1+o_{n}(1))n^{2}2^{-n}.

Thus Corollary 1.2 proves the Rademacher singularity conjecture stated as Conjecture 1.1 in [30]. Together with the result of Jain, Sah and Sawhney [10] for nonuniform laws, it establishes the finite support singularity conjecture for every fixed nonconstant finitely supported real distribution.

To deduce the corollary, let ℰn\mathcal{E}_{n} be the union of the elementary events entering (1.1). Lemma 5.4 gives

0≤an​(S)−ℙ⁡(ℰn)≤C​n4​q−2​n.\displaystyle 0\leq a_{n}(S)-\mathbb{P}\left(\mathcal{E}_{n}\right)\leq Cn^{4}q^{-2n}.

Since ℰn\mathcal{E}_{n} implies singularity, this lower bound and (1.2) at z=0z=0 prove the corollary. For S={0,1}S=\{0,1\}, the additional term from opposite pairs n⁡(n−1)​4−nn(n-1)4^{-n} is absorbed in the stated error.

Edelman [2] identified n−1/2n^{-1/2} as the natural scale of the least singular value for matrices with independent standard Gaussian entries. Following work of Rudelson [24], Rudelson and Vershynin [21, 22] established the same scale for independent identically distributed subgaussian entries with mean zero and variance one, with a lower tail bound of the form C​ε+e−c​nC\varepsilon+e^{-cn} at radius εn−1/2\varepsilon n^{-1/2}. In recent work, Sah, Sahasrabudhe and Sawhney [25] refined the coefficient of the linear term to 1+o⁡(1)1+o(1).

For the uniform finite supports considered here, Theorem 1.1 has the natural linear dependence on zz, with a constant CSC_{S} depending only on SS, and identifies the singularity contribution asymptotically as (1+o⁡(1))​an​(S)(1+o(1))a_{n}(S).

The main new ingredient is a Fourier averaging estimate in the inversion of randomness argument, valid at coefficient scales within a polynomial factor of qnq^{n}. We take moments whose order grows with nn, average over the coefficients, and classify the resulting sets of approximate linear relations by dimension and density. The estimate balances the decay of the integrand against the volume of the corresponding frequency regions.

For arbitrary real supports, a further difficulty at this polynomial scale is that bases drawn from finite product sets need not admit useful determinant bounds as the dimension grows. We obtain a count of possible output labels that is independent of the inverse norm of the interpolation basis, using a recursive reduction that retains the original input labels. We also construct many bases with well conditioned initial segments, so that the number of completion directions contributing a loss at the localization scale is controlled by the density loss. Averaging over these bases yields a weighted cover of the frequency regions. The resulting counting and inverse Jacobian costs are absorbed by the additional decay supplied by the density loss.

We discuss this difficulty and our treatment of it in Section 2.2. For algebraic supports, a lower bound on nonzero determinants gives a simpler approach to this part of the argument. Appendix A gives this bound and its proof; it is not used in the proof of the main theorem.

Section 2 explains why polynomial precision is required and describes the counting and geometric estimates underlying the argument.

1.2. Organization

Section 2 explains the proof and the difficulties arising from uniform distributions and arbitrary real supports. Section 3 proves the counting and geometric estimates. Section 4 establishes the Fourier averaging theorem. Section 5 applies it to random normal vectors and completes the proof of the main theorem, using the estimate of Jain, Sah and Sawhney [10] for structured vectors. Appendix A records the determinant estimate available for algebraic supports.

2. Outline of the proof

The main new ingredient is an averaging estimate that refines Tikhomirov’s inversion of randomness at polynomial precision. We first explain the precision required by the reduction and the obstruction in the uniform case, and then describe the additional difficulty for arbitrary real supports.

We use Tikhomirov’s reduction by inversion of randomness; see Sections 2, 4 and 5 in [32]. At a concentration scale TT, an incompressible normal is rescaled and rounded to an integer vector in an admissible product set at scale N=Θ⁡(T−1)N=\Theta(T^{-1}). The required counting estimate is therefore a bound for coefficient vectors whose random linear forms have large concentration. The critical point is that the estimate must hold in the range

1≤N≤qn​(n+1)−D,D>1,\displaystyle 1\leq N\leq q^{n}(n+1)^{-D},\qquad D>1,

for every fixed D>1D>1. A range separated from qnq^{n} by a fixed exponential factor gives the sharp exponential rate, but not the polynomial precision in Theorem 1.1.

In this section, EE denotes a translate of SS containing zero. For fixed coefficients, translating the support only translates the linear form and does not change its concentration function.

2.1. Inversion of randomness at polynomial scales

Proposition 4.5 and Corollary 4.3 in [32] use repeated random averaging to control the concentration of random sums whose coefficients are discretized candidate normal vectors. At each step, the concentration bound is updated after averaging over one more random coefficient. For the Bernoulli(1/2)(1/2) coefficient law used in that reduction, the averaging operators have the form

gj​(t)=12​gj−1​(t)+12​gj−1​(t+Xj).\displaystyle g_{j}(t)=\frac{1}{2}g_{j-1}(t)+\frac{1}{2}g_{j-1}(t+X_{j}).

A bound with a fixed loss η>0\eta>0 at each averaging step produces

(12+η)j=2−j​(1+2​η)j.\displaystyle\left(\frac{1}{2}+\eta\right)^{j}=2^{-j}(1+2\eta)^{j}.

For fixed η\eta this has an exponential cost. Taking the auxiliary loss arbitrarily small gives a sharp exponential rate, but supplies no uniform estimate when that loss decreases with nn. At the scale of n2​2−nn^{2}2^{-n} the accumulated loss must instead be polynomial, requiring a refinement of this estimate with a fixed loss. The comparison used by Jain, Sah and Sawhney [10] relies on a strict inequality between the exponential scale of the estimate for unstructured vectors and the probability that two entries agree. If pa=ℙ⁡(ξ=a)p_{a}=\mathbb{P}\left(\xi=a\right) and H(ξ)=−∑apalogpaH(\xi)=-\sum_{a}p_{a}\log p_{a}, then

e−H⁡(ξ)≤∑apa2,\displaystyle e^{-H(\xi)}\leq\sum_{a}p_{a}^{2},

with equality precisely when ξ\xi is uniform on its support. For a nonuniform law, the strict inequality allows the unstructured contribution to be exponentially smaller than the elementary contribution from pairs of rows. For a uniform law both bases equal q−1q^{-1}, so this comparison does not yield the required smaller remainder.

We retain the discretization by product sets from [32] and use a Fourier averaging estimate at the required polynomial scale. The underlying small ball problem goes back to Littlewood and Offord [14] and Erdős [3]. Fourier estimates for concentration functions appear in the work of Esseen [4] and Halász [8]; Friedland and Sodin [7] give an analytic approach relating small ball bounds to Diophantine approximation.

In our argument, Fourier analysis is combined with averaging over the random coefficients to show that, for a coefficient vector chosen from an admissible product set at scale NN, the probability that the corresponding random sum has concentration larger than L/NL/N is at most e−M​ne^{-Mn}. Here LL is independent of MM and DD. For every fixed D>1D>1 and arbitrarily large M≥1M\geq 1, the estimate holds uniformly over N≤qn​(n+1)−DN\leq q^{n}(n+1)^{-D} once nn is sufficiently large. We first reduce this problem to bounding the supremum of a smoothed density FZF_{Z}, where ZZ is a continuous perturbation of the original coefficient vector.

Fourier inversion expresses FZF_{Z} as an integral involving

φ⁡(t)=q−1​∑a∈Ee2​π​i​a​t,ΦZ​(θ)=∏i=1nφ⁡(Zi​θ).\displaystyle\varphi(t)=q^{-1}\sum_{a\in E}e^{2\pi iat},\qquad\Phi_{Z}(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\varphi(Z_{i}\theta).

We split this integral into low, intermediate, and far frequencies. The low-frequency contribution is bounded by C/(N​n)C/(N\sqrt{n}) directly from admissibility. For intermediate frequencies, a fixed moment estimate, followed by averaging over ZZ, gives an exceptional probability at most e−M​ne^{-Mn}. It remains to prove a comparable bound for the far-frequency contribution RZR_{Z}:

ℙZ​(‖RZ‖∞>1N​n)≤e−M​n.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{Z}\!\left(\|R_{Z}\|_{\infty}>\frac{1}{N\sqrt{n}}\right)\leq e^{-Mn}.

This is the main part of the argument. We first apply Fourier inversion, then take a high even moment, and finally average over the random coefficients. More precisely, we bound the supremum of RZR_{Z} by its spatial moment of even order k=Θ⁡(n/log⁡n)k=\Theta(n/\log n). Integrating in the spatial variable imposes the constraint

θ1+⋯+θk=0,\displaystyle\theta_{1}+\cdots+\theta_{k}=0,

so the resulting Fourier integral is over

Hk={θ∈ℝk:θ1+⋯+θk=0}.\displaystyle H_{k}=\{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{k}:\theta_{1}+\cdots+\theta_{k}=0\}.

After replacing the coefficient densities by suitable smooth majorants, independence allows us to average each coefficient separately. The resulting factors have the form

Ki​(θ)=q−k​∑v∈Ekν^i​(−⟨v,θ⟩).\displaystyle K_{i}(\theta)=q^{-k}\sum_{v\in E^{k}}\widehat{\nu}_{i}(-\langle v,\theta\rangle).

The Fourier transforms ν^i\widehat{\nu}_{i} decay away from zero, so the kernel bounds depend on how many vectors v∈Ekv\in E^{k} make ⟨v,θ⟩\langle v,\theta\rangle small. For a fixed frequency vector θ\theta, we call v∈Ekv\in E^{k} an approximate relation vector if

|⟨v,θ⟩|≤R/N,\displaystyle|\langle v,\theta\rangle|\leq R/N,

where RR is a parameter chosen later. Thus the number of approximate relations means the number of such vectors vv, not the number of linearly independent relations. This converts the moment estimate into a problem about the number and structure of approximate relation vectors. We write V⁡(θ)V(\theta) for this set.

There are two sources of smallness in this integral. If few approximate relations occur, the kernel factors are small, giving a good bound. If many relations occur, they restrict the frequencies to a small region. To use both effects, we group frequencies according to the dimension of a subspace close to V⁡(θ)V(\theta) and the number of these vectors. Write rr for this dimension and d=k−rd=k-r. The construction in Lemma 4.8 ensures that |V⁡(θ)|≤qr|V(\theta)|\leq q^{r}. We define the integer density loss tt by

q−t−1<|V⁡(θ)|qr≤q−t.\displaystyle q^{-t-1}<\frac{|V(\theta)|}{q^{r}}\leq q^{-t}.

The counting estimates of Section 3 are applied in Section 4 with u=t+1u=t+1, since |V⁡(θ)|>qr−u|V(\theta)|>q^{r-u}.

A related classification of hyperplanes by the number of cube vertices they contain was used by Kahn, Komlós and Szemerédi [11] and Tao and Vu [30]. Here we record both the dimension rr of the selected approximate relation space and the ratio |V⁡(θ)|/qr|V(\theta)|/q^{r}, since both enter the Fourier integral estimate.

When the density loss is bounded, the localization estimates show that the relation vectors lie in an exact subspace UU. Moreover, the far-frequency restriction forces UU to contain no coordinate vector. Theorem 3.1 then gives d≥k/2−O⁡(1)d\geq k/2-O(1) and bounds the number of possible spaces by

exp⁡{d​log⁡(k+1)+Oq,u​(k)},\displaystyle\exp\!\left\{d\log(k+1)+O_{q,u}(k)\right\},

where uu is bounded and |U∩Ek|≥qk−d−u|U\cap E^{k}|\geq q^{k-d-u}. For each fixed space, we estimate the integral in coordinates adapted to its relations. Combining this integral estimate with the count of possible spaces produces the terms

d​log⁡(k+1)−d​log⁡(qn/N).\displaystyle d\log(k+1)-d\log(q^{n}/N).

Since N≤qn​(n+1)−DN\leq q^{n}(n+1)^{-D}, their leading contribution is

−(D−1)​d​log⁡n.\displaystyle-(D-1)d\log n.

With d≥k/2−O⁡(1)d\geq k/2-O(1) and a sufficiently large constant in the choice k=Θ⁡(n/log⁡n)k=\Theta(n/\log n), this gives the required exponential bound. The coefficient one in the counting estimate is therefore what allows every fixed D>1D>1.

For large density loss, the kernel already supplies a strong additional saving, so a coarser count is sufficient. We cover the frequency region by sets defined by approximate relations from selected bases. The estimates in Section 3 provide many suitable bases and control the number of possible output labels for each input basis. Averaging over these bases controls the total weight of the cover and the cost of the changes of variables used to integrate over it. The saving from the density loss absorbs these costs.

Finally, we choose the moment order and the threshold separating the two regimes, and sum over all possible codimensions and density losses. This proves the far-frequency estimate and completes the proof of Theorem 4.2.

2.2. Real supports

For arbitrary real supports, a basis chosen from a finite product set may be nearly linearly dependent, with no usable lower bound on its determinant as the dimension grows. At each fixed dimension, the nonzero determinants have a positive minimum, but this minimum need not have a lower bound suitable for the exponentially small radii in our argument. Approximating the support by rational or algebraic sets does not by itself give such a bound: the constants depend on the approximating set and need not remain controlled as the approximation is refined.

The exact span of the relation vectors is a natural first choice, but it may not contain a basis for which the Fourier change of variables has a sufficiently small inverse Jacobian. For algebraic supports, a field norm gives a determinant lower bound exp⁡{−OE​(k​log⁡(k+1))}\exp\{-O_{E}(k\log(k+1))\}; see Appendix A. For general real supports, we control the inverse Jacobian through the following three constructions.

First, at precision η=exp⁡{−C​log2⁡(k+1)}\eta=\exp\{-C\log^{2}(k+1)\}, we maximize scaled projected volumes over all dimensions. The comparison with the preceding dimension bounds the inverse Gram matrix of the selected frame. Comparison with the next dimension puts every remaining relation within distance η\eta of its span. The selected space may be smaller than the exact span. A maximal coordinate minor then gives a graph with bounded coefficients and distinct input labels in a product set. The selected vectors provide an input basis whose least singular value is ΩE​(η/k3)\Omega_{E}(\eta/k^{3}).

Second, Proposition 3.2 bounds the number of possible output labels by

exp⁡{OE​(k⁡(u+1)+d​log⁡(d+1))}.\displaystyle\exp\{O_{E}(k(u+1)+d\log(d+1))\}.

Its proof records labels from the original finite set, rather than approximating coordinates in a basis with poor conditioning. Its reduction uses the scalar Littlewood–Offord estimate of Erdős [3]; a recursive decrease of input dimension and density loss keeps both the label count and the accumulated error under control.

Third, Lemma 3.7 constructs many bases with bounded interpolation coefficients. A projection estimate from Hanson–Wright [23] and a second moment argument weighted by the determinant give many prefixes with least singular value ΩE​(k−1)\Omega_{E}(k^{-1}). Only OE​(u+1)O_{E}(u+1) completion directions then depend on η\eta. The number of prefixes permits averaging slab indicators before integration. The resulting loss from the inverse Jacobian is bounded by

exp⁡{OE​(k​log⁡(k+1)+(u+1)​log2⁡(k+1))}.\displaystyle\exp\{O_{E}(k\log(k+1)+(u+1)\log^{2}(k+1))\}.

In the frequency decomposition the counting lemmas are applied with u=t+1u=t+1, while the kernel product contributes q−n​tq^{-nt}. For large tt, the negative term −n​t​log⁡q-nt\log q absorbs the displayed cost. For bounded tt, localization makes the graph exact, allowing the count with coefficient one in front of d​log⁡(k+1)d\log(k+1).

Finally, the passage from Theorem 4.2 to random normals uses the random rounding and inversion of randomness construction of Sections 2 and 5 in [32]. We use the decomposition into compressible and incompressible vectors due to Rudelson and Vershynin [21]; the contribution from almost constant vectors is controlled by the estimate of Jain, Sah and Sawhney [10], used in Lemma 5.1 below. For an incompressible normal, Theorem 4.2 controls the expected last scale at which its concentration exceeds a fixed linear bound. Conditioning on all the other columns gives the small ball estimate in Proposition 5.3, and the deterministic argument using distances to column spans in Section 5 completes the proof of Theorem 1.1.

3. Counting linear relations in finite product sets

The high-moment argument in Section 4 requires two counting estimates for linear constraints on finite product sets. The first counts subspaces containing many points of EkE^{k}. Writing such a subspace as a graph

U={(x,A​x):x∈ℝr},\displaystyle U=\{(x,Ax):x\in\mathbb{R}^{r}\},

its points in EkE^{k} correspond to inputs x∈Erx\in E^{r} satisfying the exact constraint A​x∈EdAx\in E^{d}.

The second estimate allows an error in this constraint. For a fixed invertible input matrix W∈Er×rW\in E^{r\times r}, it counts output matrices Y∈Ed×rY\in E^{d\times r} for which

dist∞⁡(Y​W−1​x,Ed)≤ε\displaystyle\operatorname{dist}_{\infty}(YW^{-1}x,E^{d})\leq\varepsilon

holds for many inputs x∈Erx\in E^{r}. Thus, in this section, “exact” and “approximate” refer to whether the linear constraints are satisfied exactly or up to a prescribed error. The quantities being counted are subspaces in the first estimate and output matrices in the second.

These estimates will be applied to sets of approximate relation vectors arising in the Fourier argument. We also prove that a dense subset of ErE^{r} contains many bases with controlled interpolation coefficients and determinants.

Equivalently, if XX is uniform on EkE^{k}, then

q−k​|U∩Ek|=ℙ⁡(X∈U).\displaystyle q^{-k}|U\cap E^{k}|=\mathbb{P}(X\in U).

Thus the first estimate may be viewed as a Littlewood–Offord type counting problem, in which the relevant subspaces are classified by their dimension and intersection density.

Direct counting estimates for vectors with large concentration were developed by Ferber, Jain, Luh and Samotij [5]. Here the objects to be counted are the spaces of relations among the frequencies in a Fourier moment.

Throughout this section E⊂ℝE\subset\mathbb{R} is fixed, |E|=q≥2|E|=q\geq 2, and 0∈E0\in E. Write Δ=mina≠b∈E⁡|a−b|>0\Delta=\min_{a\neq b\in E}|a-b|>0. Let ℋd​(k,u)\mathcal{H}_{d}(k,u) be the logarithm of the number of subspaces UU of codimension dd satisfying U=span⁡(U∩Ek)U=\operatorname{span}(U\cap E^{k}) and |U∩Ek|≥qk−d−u|U\cap E^{k}|\geq q^{k-d-u}.

Theorem 3.1.

There are constants C3.1,c3.1>0C_{\ref{thm:count}},c_{\ref{thm:count}}>0 depending only on qq such that for 0≤d≤k0\leq d\leq k and u≥0u\geq 0,

ℋd​(k,u)≤d​log⁡(k+1)+C3.1​k​(u+2)2​q2​u.\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{d}(k,u)\leq d\log(k+1)+C_{\ref{thm:count}}k(u+2)^{2}q^{2u}. (3.1)

If U⊂ℝkU\subset\mathbb{R}^{k} has codimension dd and contains no coordinate vector, then

|U∩Ek|qk−d≤(1+c3.1(k−2d)+)−1/2.\displaystyle\frac{|U\cap E^{k}|}{q^{k-d}}\leq\left(1+c_{\ref{thm:count}}(k-2d)_{+}\right)^{-1/2}. (3.2)

After choosing an injective projection onto rr coordinates, write U={(x,A​x):x∈ℝr}U=\{(x,Ax):x\in\mathbb{R}^{r}\} with A∈ℝd×rA\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}, where d=k−rd=k-r. Its points in EkE^{k} correspond to

𝒮⁡(A)={x∈Er:A​x∈Ed}.\displaystyle\mathcal{S}(A)=\{x\in E^{r}:Ax\in E^{d}\}.

They span UU exactly when 𝒮⁡(A)\mathcal{S}(A) spans ℝr\mathbb{R}^{r}.

The first estimate retains coefficient one in front of d​log⁡(k+1)d\log(k+1) for bounded uu. The second will force d≥k/2−Oq,u​(1)d\geq k/2-O_{q,u}(1) once coordinate directions have been excluded. For k=2​mk=2m, the space given by x2​j−1=x2​jx_{2j-1}=x_{2j} has dimension mm, contains qmq^{m} points of EkE^{k} and no coordinate vector. Taking a fixed nonzero element of EE on one pair and zero elsewhere shows that these points span the space. Different perfect matchings give different such spaces, since two coordinate functionals agree identically exactly when they are paired. There are (2​m)!/(2m​m!)(2m)!/(2^{m}m!) matchings, whose logarithm is m​log⁡(2​m)+O⁡(m)m\log(2m)+O(m). This matches the leading entropy coefficient in this regime.

Our second estimate concerns approximate relations. The columns of an invertible matrix W∈Er×rW\in E^{r\times r} specify the inputs of a linear map, and the columns of Y∈Ed×rY\in E^{d\times r} specify its values on those inputs. We count the possible YY for which the map sends many further points of ErE^{r} close to EdE^{d}.

Proposition 3.2.

There are constants C3.2′=C3.2′​(E)>0C^{\prime}_{\ref{prop:approxcount}}=C^{\prime}_{\ref{prop:approxcount}}(E)>0 and C3.2>0C_{\ref{prop:approxcount}}>0 depending only on qq such that the following holds. Let r≥1r\geq 1 and d≥0d\geq 0 be integers with K=r+d≥2K=r+d\geq 2 and ε=exp⁡[−C3.2′​log2⁡(K+1)]\varepsilon=\exp[-C^{\prime}_{\ref{prop:approxcount}}\log^{2}(K+1)]. For every invertible W∈Er×rW\in E^{r\times r} and u≥0u\geq 0, the number of Y∈Ed×rY\in E^{d\times r} satisfying

|{x∈Er:dist∞⁡(Y​W−1​x,Ed)≤ε}|≥qr−u\displaystyle\left|\{x\in E^{r}:\operatorname{dist}_{\infty}(YW^{-1}x,E^{d})\leq\varepsilon\}\right|\geq q^{r-u}

is at most

exp⁡{C3.2​[K⁡(u+1)+d​log⁡(d+1)]}.\displaystyle\exp\{C_{\ref{prop:approxcount}}[K(u+1)+d\log(d+1)]\}.

We prove Theorem 3.1 first. The proof of Proposition 3.2 uses a reduction of the input dimension, followed by induction on the number of output rows.

3.1. Counting subspaces

For an affine subspace L⊂ℝkL\subset\mathbb{R}^{k} and any finite F⊂ℝF\subset\mathbb{R}, an injective coordinate projection gives

|L∩Fk|≤|F|dimL.\displaystyle|L\cap F^{k}|\leq|F|^{\dim L}. (3.3)

Indeed, choose coordinate functionals forming a basis on its direction space; their joint restriction to LL is injective. Thus |U∩Ek|≥qr−u|U\cap E^{k}|\geq q^{r-u} expresses a loss of at most quq^{u} from the maximum qrq^{r} for a subspace of dimension rr. The assumption 0∈E0\in E makes coordinate subspaces examples with zero density loss.

We use the following form of the Littlewood–Offord estimate both for exact relations and for approximate ones.

Lemma 3.3.

There is a constant C3.3>0C_{\ref{lem:scalar}}>0 depending only on qq such that the following holds. Let bib_{i} be independent random variables uniformly distributed on EE. If at least s≥1s\geq 1 coefficients satisfy |ai|>2​h/Δ|a_{i}|>2h/\Delta, where h≥0h\geq 0, then

ℒ⁡(∑iai​bi,h)≤C3.3/s.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\left(\sum_{i}a_{i}b_{i},h\right)\leq C_{\ref{lem:scalar}}/\sqrt{s}.
Proof.

Choose a set II of ss indices satisfying |ai|​Δ>2​h|a_{i}|\Delta>2h. Suppose first that h>0h>0. For each i∈Ii\in I, distinct points of ai​Ea_{i}E are separated by more than 2​h2h, so

ℒ⁡(ai​bi,h)=q−1.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(a_{i}b_{i},h)=q^{-1}.

Adding independent summands cannot increase concentration. The Kolmogorov–Rogozin inequality (Theorem 1 in [20]) then gives

ℒ⁡(∑iai​bi,h)≤ℒ⁡(∑i∈Iai​bi,h)≤C∑i∈I(1−ℒ⁡(ai​bi,h))=Cs⁡(1−q−1)≤2​Cs,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\left(\sum_{i}a_{i}b_{i},h\right)\leq\mathcal{L}\left(\sum_{i\in I}a_{i}b_{i},h\right)\leq\frac{C}{\sqrt{\sum_{i\in I}(1-\mathcal{L}(a_{i}b_{i},h))}}=\frac{C}{\sqrt{s(1-q^{-1})}}\leq\frac{\sqrt{2}C}{\sqrt{s}},

where CC is an absolute constant.

If h=0h=0, choose h′>0h^{\prime}>0 such that 2​h′<Δ​mini∈I​|ai|2h^{\prime}<\Delta\min_{i\in I}|a_{i}|. Applying the preceding argument at radius h′h^{\prime} and using ℒ⁡(X,0)≤ℒ⁡(X,h′)\mathcal{L}(X,0)\leq\mathcal{L}(X,h^{\prime}) proves the same bound. ∎

Before proving Theorem 3.1, we establish a lemma that bounds the number of coefficient vectors on a fixed set of coordinates.

Lemma 3.4.

Let E⊂ℝE\subset\mathbb{R} have cardinality q≥2q\geq 2, and write

𝒮⁡(a)={b∈Ep:⟨a,b⟩∈E}(a∈ℝp).\displaystyle\mathcal{S}(a)=\{b\in E^{p}:\langle a,b\rangle\in E\}\qquad(a\in\mathbb{R}^{p}).

There is a constant C3.4>0C_{\ref{lem:row-count}}>0 depending only on qq such that for every integer p≥0p\geq 0 and every u≥0u\geq 0,

|{a∈ℝp:span𝒮(a)=ℝp,|𝒮(a)|≥qp−u}|≤exp{C3.4(p+1)(u+1)}.\displaystyle\left|\left\{a\in\mathbb{R}^{p}:\operatorname{span}\mathcal{S}(a)=\mathbb{R}^{p},\quad|\mathcal{S}(a)|\geq q^{p-u}\right\}\right|\leq\exp\{C_{\ref{lem:row-count}}(p+1)(u+1)\}.

Λ={x/y:x,y∈E−E,y≠0}.\displaystyle\Lambda=\{x/y:x,y\in E-E,\ y\neq 0\}.

q−u−1≤|𝒮⁡(a)|qp+1=ℙ⁡(⟨a,b⟩=c)≤q−g−1,\displaystyle q^{-u-1}\leq\frac{|\mathcal{S}(a)|}{q^{p+1}}=\mathbb{P}(\langle a,b\rangle=c)\leq q^{-g-1},

−δ0+∑ℓ=1gaiℓ​δℓ+aj​δ∗=0,aj=δ0δ∗−∑ℓ=1gaiℓ​δℓδ∗,\displaystyle-\delta_{0}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{g}a_{i_{\ell}}\delta_{\ell}+a_{j}\delta_{*}=0,\qquad a_{j}=\frac{\delta_{0}}{\delta_{*}}-\sum_{\ell=1}^{g}a_{i_{\ell}}\frac{\delta_{\ell}}{\delta_{*}},

a=P+G​V,P∈Λp,V∈Λg×p,\displaystyle a=P+GV,\qquad P\in\Lambda^{p},\quad V\in\Lambda^{g\times p},

where the columns of VV indexed by II form IgI_{g}.

If g≥1g\geq 1, the spanning assumption and rank⁡V=g\operatorname{rank}V=g allow us to choose z1,…,zg∈𝒮⁡(a)z_{1},\ldots,z_{g}\in\mathcal{S}(a) such that Z=(z1,…,zg)Z=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{g}) has V​ZVZ invertible. Writing y=a​Z∈Egy=aZ\in E^{g}, we recover

G=(y−P​Z)​(V​Z)−1.\displaystyle G=(y-PZ)(VZ)^{-1}.

Thus (P,V,Z,y)(P,V,Z,y) determines aa, without any additional record of II. For fixed gg, the number of possible data is at most |Λ|p+g​p​qp​g+g|\Lambda|^{p+gp}q^{pg+g}. When g=0g=0, we simply have a=Pa=P, giving the same bound. Consequently,

|{a∈ℝp:span𝒮(a)=ℝp,|𝒮(a)|≥qp−u}|≤∑g=0min⁡(p,⌊u⌋)|Λ|p+g​p​qp​g+g≤exp⁡{C⁡(p+1)​(u+1)},\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \left|\left\{a\in\mathbb{R}^{p}:\operatorname{span}\mathcal{S}(a)=\mathbb{R}^{p},\ |\mathcal{S}(a)|\geq q^{p-u}\right\}\right|&\leq\sum_{g=0}^{\min(p,\lfloor u\rfloor)}|\Lambda|^{p+gp}q^{pg+g}\\ &\leq\exp\{C(p+1)(u+1)\},\end{aligned}

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

We first prove (3.1). Throughout the proof, c,C>0c,C>0 depend only on qq and may change from line to line. Let r=k−dr=k-d. q−u≤ℙ⁡(⟨a,b⟩∈E)≤q​Cs.\displaystyle q^{-u}\leq\mathbb{P}(\langle a,b\rangle\in E)\leq\frac{qC}{\sqrt{s}}.

q−u≤ℙ⁡(all selected row constraints hold)≤(1−q−2)h.\displaystyle q^{-u}\leq\mathbb{P}(\text{all selected row constraints hold})\leq(1-q^{-2})^{h}.

There are at most 2k2^{k} choices of input coordinates, at most 2r2^{r} choices of JJ with |J|≤m|J|\leq m, and at most (r+1)d(r+1)^{d} choices of the additional coordinate, or its absence, for each row. ℋd​(k,u)≤(k+r)​log⁡2+d​log⁡(r+1)+C​d​(m+2)​(u+1)≤d​log⁡(k+1)+C​k​(u+2)2​q2​u.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \mathcal{H}_{d}(k,u)&\leq(k+r)\log 2+d\log(r+1)+Cd(m+2)(u+1)\\ &\leq d\log(k+1)+Ck(u+2)^{2}q^{2u}.\end{aligned}

ℙ⁡(X+γ​ξ3=t)≤1q​(1q+(q−1)​q−1q2)=1q​(1−q−1q2).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(X+\gamma\xi_{3}=t)\leq\frac{1}{q}\left(\frac{1}{q}+(q-1)\frac{q-1}{q^{2}}\right)=\frac{1}{q}\left(1-\frac{q-1}{q^{2}}\right).

3.2. Approximate interpolation and bases

To prove Proposition 3.2, we count the original rows of YY, which belong to ErE^{r}, rather than approximate the coefficient rows of Y​W−1YW^{-1}. This avoids errors amplified by a poorly conditioned input matrix WW. The argument successively reduces the input dimension while retaining these original rows. During the reduction, the rows may lie close to a low-dimensional affine subspace rather than exactly in it. We therefore need the following extension of (3.3).

Let L⊂ℝrL\subset\mathbb{R}^{r} be an affine subspace of dimension ℓ\ell. If 0≤ρ≤Δ/[4​(r+1)]0\leq\rho\leq\Delta/[4(r+1)], then

|{a∈Er:dist∞⁡(a,L)≤ρ}|≤qℓ.\displaystyle\left|\{a\in E^{r}:\operatorname{dist}_{\infty}(a,L)\leq\rho\}\right|\leq q^{\ell}. (3.4)

For ℓ=r\ell=r, this is immediate. Otherwise, choose a basis matrix for the direction space of LL, and select ℓ\ell rows whose determinant has maximal absolute value. Using the corresponding coordinates as inputs, write

L={(x,A​x+b):x∈ℝℓ}.\displaystyle L=\{(x,Ax+b):x\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell}\}.

Maximality of the chosen minor gives |Ai​j|≤1|A_{ij}|\leq 1: replacing one selected row by an output row multiplies the determinant by the corresponding entry of AA.

If (x,y)∈Er(x,y)\in E^{r} satisfies dist∞⁡((x,y),L)≤ρ\operatorname{dist}_{\infty}((x,y),L)\leq\rho, choose (x′,A​x′+b)∈L(x^{\prime},Ax^{\prime}+b)\in L within distance ρ\rho. Then

‖y−A​x−b‖∞≤‖y−A​x′−b‖∞+‖A⁡(x′−x)‖∞≤(ℓ+1)​ρ.\displaystyle\|y-Ax-b\|_{\infty}\leq\|y-Ax^{\prime}-b\|_{\infty}+\|A(x^{\prime}-x)\|_{\infty}\leq(\ell+1)\rho.

Thus two points (x,y),(x,y~)∈Er(x,y),(x,\widetilde{y})\in E^{r} within distance ρ\rho of LL, with the same input coordinates, satisfy

‖y−y~‖∞≤2​(ℓ+1)​ρ<Δ.\displaystyle\|y-\widetilde{y}\|_{\infty}\leq 2(\ell+1)\rho<\Delta.

Since distinct elements of EE are separated by at least Δ\Delta, we must have y=y~y=\widetilde{y}. Projection onto the ℓ\ell input coordinates is therefore injective on the set being counted, proving (3.4). The same argument applies when ℓ=0\ell=0, with no input coordinates.

The next lemma provides the dimension reduction used in the count. Starting from mm output rows and pp input coordinates, it selects some input coordinates and hh output rows to form a new input vector of dimension p′≤Cq​mp^{\prime}\leq C_{q}m. If the original system has at least qp−vq^{p-v} approximate solutions, the reduced system has at least qp′−(v−2​h)q^{p^{\prime}-(v-2h)}. Thus recording hh output rows reduces the density loss by at least 2​h2h, which will offset the cost of recording these rows in the recursive count. The approximation affects the linear map; the retained coordinates and selected output labels still determine the full output label exactly.

Lemma 3.5.

There are constants C3.5≥1C_{\ref{lem:compression}}\geq 1 depending only on qq and C3.5′,c3.5>0C^{\prime}_{\ref{lem:compression}},c_{\ref{lem:compression}}>0 depending only on EE with the following property. Let B∈ℝm×pB\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}, m,p≥1m,p\geq 1, v≥0v\geq 0, and 0<ε≤c3.5​(m+p)−40<\varepsilon\leq c_{\ref{lem:compression}}(m+p)^{-4}. Suppose 𝒮⊂Ep\mathcal{S}\subset E^{p}, |𝒮|≥qp−v|\mathcal{S}|\geq q^{p-v}, and f:𝒮→Emf:\mathcal{S}\to E^{m} satisfy ∥B​x−f⁡(x)∥∞≤ε\lVert Bx-f(x)\rVert_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon. There are sets J⊂[p]J\subset[p] and I⊂[m]I\subset[m], with h=|I|h=|I| and p′=|J|+hp^{\prime}=|J|+h, such that

p′≤min⁡(p,C3.5​m),2​h≤v.\displaystyle p^{\prime}\leq\min(p,C_{\ref{lem:compression}}m),\qquad 2h\leq v.

The map T​x=(xJ,BI​x)Tx=(x_{J},B_{I}x) has full row rank and a right inverse UU determined by J,I,BIJ,I,B_{I}. With B′=B​UB^{\prime}=BU, we have

∥B−B′​T∥2→∞≤C3.5′​(m+p)5/2​ε.\displaystyle\lVert B-B^{\prime}T\rVert_{2\to\infty}\leq C^{\prime}_{\ref{lem:compression}}(m+p)^{5/2}\varepsilon.

For ψ⁡(x)=(xJ,fI​(x))\psi(x)=(x_{J},f_{I}(x)), the value f⁡(x)f(x) is determined by ψ⁡(x)\psi(x), and

|ψ⁡(𝒮)|≥qp′−(v−2​h),∥B′​ψ​(x)−f⁡(x)∥∞≤C3.5′​(m+p)3​ε.\displaystyle|\psi(\mathcal{S})|\geq q^{p^{\prime}-(v-2h)},\qquad\lVert B^{\prime}\psi(x)-f(x)\rVert_{\infty}\leq C^{\prime}_{\ref{lem:compression}}(m+p)^{3}\varepsilon.
Proof.

We first obtain anticoncentration from several disjoint rectangular column blocks. Repeatedly halving the number of singular values above the current threshold then either finds these blocks or removes only Oq​(m)O_{q}(m) columns. Rows of maximal volume provide the reduction with bounded regression coefficients.

A small ball estimate. A related replication argument for vector anti-concentration appears in the work of Ferber, Jain and Zhao [6] on Hadamard matrices. We include the short block version needed here. Fix an even integer LL, to be chosen using only qq. Suppose an h×ph\times p matrix DD contains LL disjoint blocks GℓG_{\ell}, each with j=⌈h/2⌉j=\lceil h/2\rceil columns and smin​(Gℓ)≥κ>0s_{\min}(G_{\ell})\geq\kappa>0. For bb uniform on EpE^{p}, Gaussian majorization followed by Fourier inversion gives

ℙ⁡(∥D​b−y∥2≤ρ​h)≤eh/2​∫ℝh∏i|φ⁡(⟨D⋅i,t⟩/ρ)|​d​γh​(t),\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\lVert Db-y\rVert_{2}\leq\rho\sqrt{h}\right)\leq e^{h/2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{h}}\prod_{i}|\varphi(\langle D_{\cdot i},t\rangle/\rho)|\,d\gamma_{h}(t),

where φ⁡(t)=𝔼​ei​t​b1\varphi(t)=\mathbb{E}e^{itb_{1}} and γh\gamma_{h} is standard Gaussian measure. Discard unselected factors and apply Hölder with LL equal exponents to the disjoint blocks. For each block, expanding the even power |φ|L|\varphi|^{L} and integrating the Gaussian gives

∫∏i∈Gℓ|φ(⟨D⋅i,t⟩/ρ)|Ldγh(t)=𝔼e−∥Gℓζ∥22/(2ρ2)≤∏i=1j𝔼e−κ2ζi2/(2ρ2).\displaystyle\int\prod_{i\in G_{\ell}}|\varphi(\langle D_{\cdot i},t\rangle/\rho)|^{L}\,d\gamma_{h}(t)=\mathbb{E}e^{-\lVert G_{\ell}\zeta\rVert_{2}^{2}/(2\rho^{2})}\leq\prod_{i=1}^{j}\mathbb{E}e^{-\kappa^{2}\zeta_{i}^{2}/(2\rho^{2})}.

The ζi\zeta_{i} are independent, each a sum of L/2L/2 independent differences of independent random variables uniformly distributed on EE. Lemma 3.3 gives ℒ⁡(ζi,Δ/4)≤C/L\mathcal{L}(\zeta_{i},\Delta/4)\leq C/\sqrt{L}. Partitioning the real line into intervals of length Δ/2\Delta/2, and summing the suprema of the Gaussian on these intervals, shows that

𝔼e−ζi2/(2a2)≤C/L(0<a≤cΔ).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}e^{-\zeta_{i}^{2}/(2a^{2})}\leq C/\sqrt{L}\qquad(0<a\leq c\Delta).

The sum of these Gaussian suprema is bounded by an absolute constant in this range. Thus the preceding small ball probability is at most eh/2​(C/L)je^{h/2}(C/\sqrt{L})^{j} when ρ≤c​Δ​κ\rho\leq c\Delta\kappa. Fix L=L⁡(q)L=L(q) large enough that this is at most q−3​hq^{-3h} for every h≥1h\geq 1.

Choosing the coordinates and rows. Set δ0=C′​ε​m​p\delta_{0}=C^{\prime}\varepsilon\sqrt{mp}, where C′C^{\prime} is large enough for the preceding small ball estimate. Initially JJ is empty and the working threshold is δ0\delta_{0}. At any stage let BRB_{R} be the remaining columns, and let hh be the number of its singular values greater than the current threshold δ\delta. If h=0h=0, stop. Otherwise let HH be its top hh left singular space; then ∥(I−PH)​BR∥≤δ\lVert(I-P_{H})B_{R}\rVert\leq\delta.

Try to remove, temporarily, LL disjoint groups of j=⌈h/2⌉j=\lceil h/2\rceil columns. As long as the jjth singular value of the remaining matrix exceeds 2​δ2\delta, its projection onto HH has jjth singular value greater than δ\delta. Project further onto its top jj left singular space and choose jj columns maximizing determinant. If this square matrix is D0D_{0}, write the projected matrix as D=D0​VD=D_{0}V. Replacing column ii of D0D_{0} by a projected column D⋅ℓD_{\cdot\ell} multiplies its determinant by Vi​ℓV_{i\ell}. Maximality of the absolute determinant therefore gives |Vi​ℓ|≤1|V_{i\ell}|\leq 1. There are at most pp such columns, so ∥V∥2≤∥V∥HS2≤j​p\lVert V\rVert^{2}\leq\lVert V\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\leq jp. It follows that D​DT⪯j​p​D0​D0TDD^{T}\preceq jpD_{0}D_{0}^{T}, and smin​(D0)≥δ/j​ps_{\min}(D_{0})\geq\delta/\sqrt{jp}. The same lower bound holds before the last projection.

If all LL groups are found, retain them among the remaining columns and stop. If the procedure fails, add the groups already removed at this stage permanently to JJ, double δ\delta, and start again. At failure the jjth singular value is at most 2​δ2\delta. Thus, after doubling the threshold, the number of singular values above it is at most ⌈h/2⌉−1<h/2\lceil h/2\rceil-1<h/2. The ranks encountered are bounded by m,m/2,m/4,…m,m/2,m/4,\ldots, and at a stage of rank hh fewer than L​hLh columns are added to JJ. Their total is less than 2​L​m2Lm. There are at most ⌈log2⁡(m+1)⌉\lceil\log_{2}(m+1)\rceil failures, so the threshold is at most 2​(m+1)​δ02(m+1)\delta_{0}. Consequently

|J|≤2​L​m,δ≤2​(m+1)​δ0.\displaystyle|J|\leq 2Lm,\qquad\delta\leq 2(m+1)\delta_{0}.

At termination either h=0h=0, or PH​BRP_{H}B_{R} contains the LL blocks just constructed, with least singular values at least δ/j​p\delta/\sqrt{jp}.

For h>0h>0, choose hh rows II of the actual matrix BRB_{R} maximizing their row volume; they are independent. Regress every row on these rows by orthogonal projection, writing BR=D​BI,R+E0B_{R}=DB_{I,R}+E_{0}. Let w1,…,whw_{1},\ldots,w_{h} be the selected rows and write an arbitrary row as ∑iDℓ​i​wi+eℓ\sum_{i}D_{\ell i}w_{i}+e_{\ell}, where eℓe_{\ell} is orthogonal to their span. In the wedge product obtained by replacing wiw_{i}, only the term Dℓ​i​wiD_{\ell i}w_{i} and the orthogonal term eℓe_{\ell} survive. They are orthogonal in the exterior power. Thus the squared replacement volume is at least |Dℓ​i|2​vol⁡(w1,…,wh)2|D_{\ell i}|^{2}\operatorname{vol}(w_{1},\ldots,w_{h})^{2}. The maximizing property bounds it by the original squared volume, and hence |Dℓ​i|≤1|D_{\ell i}|\leq 1. Also

∥(E0)ℓ⋅∥2≤h+1δ.\displaystyle\lVert(E_{0})_{\ell\cdot}\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{h+1}\,\delta.

For a row outside II, append it to the maximizing rows. The Gram determinant of these h+1h+1 rows is the maximal squared volume in dimension hh times its squared distance to their span. Its smallest eigenvalue is at most δ2\delta^{2}, because BRB_{R} has at most hh singular values above δ\delta. The determinant is at most δ2\delta^{2} times the hhth elementary symmetric function of its eigenvalues, which is the sum of its h+1h+1 squared row minors. Each is at most the maximal squared volume. This proves the claimed row bound; rows in II have zero residual.

The reduced system. Set T​x=(xJ,BI​x)Tx=(x_{J},B_{I}x) and B′=(BJ−D​BI,J,D)B^{\prime}=(B_{J}-DB_{I,J},D). Full row rank follows by restricting the selected rows to R=JcR=J^{c}. Set A=BI,RA=B_{I,R}. The map

U​(z,w)J=z,U​(z,w)R=AT​(A​AT)−1​(w−BI,J​z)\displaystyle U(z,w)_{J}=z,\qquad U(z,w)_{R}=A^{T}(AA^{T})^{-1}(w-B_{I,J}z)

is determined by the recorded rows and satisfies T​U=ITU=I. Orthogonality of the regression residual gives BR​AT​(A​AT)−1=DB_{R}A^{T}(AA^{T})^{-1}=D, and hence B​U=B′BU=B^{\prime}. Multiplication on JJ then gives BJ−D​BI,JB_{J}-DB_{I,J}, the other block of B′B^{\prime}. The residual B−B′​TB-B^{\prime}T is zero on JJ and equals E0E_{0} on RR. For h=0h=0 take I=∅I=\emptyset, B′=BJB^{\prime}=B_{J}, and let UU be coordinate inclusion; the residual has norm at most δ\delta. These formulas also allow p′=0p^{\prime}=0. They prove the residual estimate, p′≤pp^{\prime}\leq p and p′≤C3.5​mp^{\prime}\leq C_{\ref{lem:compression}}m with the integer C3.5=2​L+1C_{\ref{lem:compression}}=2L+1.

Since the last hh coefficients of each row of B′B^{\prime} have absolute value at most one, the row bound gives, for x∈𝒮x\in\mathcal{S},

∥B′​ψ​(x)−f⁡(x)∥∞≤(h+1)​ε+C​p​h+1​δ≤C​(m+p)3​ε.\displaystyle\lVert B^{\prime}\psi(x)-f(x)\rVert_{\infty}\leq(h+1)\varepsilon+C\sqrt{p}\sqrt{h+1}\,\delta\leq C(m+p)^{3}\varepsilon.

Choose the constant c3.5c_{\ref{lem:compression}} in the hypothesis so that the last quantity is less than Δ/4\Delta/4. Two points with the same ψ\psi then have the same entire label ff.

Fix a fiber ψ⁡(x)=(z,w)\psi(x)=(z,w), and denote its common label by f0f_{0}. Condition on the coordinates bJ=zb_{J}=z of a uniform vector b∈Epb\in E^{p}; the remaining coordinates stay independent and uniform on EE. Every point of the fiber satisfies

∥PH​(BR​bR−(f0−BJ​z))∥2≤ε​m.\displaystyle\lVert P_{H}(B_{R}b_{R}-(f_{0}-B_{J}z))\rVert_{2}\leq\varepsilon\sqrt{m}.

If h>0h>0, apply the block estimate with ρ=ε​m/h\rho=\varepsilon\sqrt{m/h} and κ=δ/j​p\kappa=\delta/\sqrt{jp}. Their ratio is at most 1/C′1/C^{\prime}, so the fiber contains at most qp−|J|−3​hq^{p-|J|-3h} points. For h=0h=0 this bound is just the size qp−|J|q^{p-|J|} of a coordinate fiber. Therefore

|ψ⁡(𝒮)|≥q|J|+3​h−v=qp′−(v−2​h).\displaystyle|\psi(\mathcal{S})|\geq q^{|J|+3h-v}=q^{p^{\prime}-(v-2h)}.

Its image lies in Ep′E^{p^{\prime}}, so comparison with qp′q^{p^{\prime}} gives 2​h≤v2h\leq v, completing the proof. ∎

Proof of Proposition 3.2.

There is only one matrix if d=0d=0, so assume d≥1d\geq 1. Write L=C3.5L=C_{\ref{lem:compression}}, which depends only on qq, and let ε0\varepsilon_{0} be the error in the statement. Throughout the recursion, the rows being counted remain the original rows of YY in ErE^{r}. Recording selected rows determines the new coordinate maps; the accompanying decrease in density loss pays for this record.

Fix the ambient row length rr. A node of the encoding has mm row labels a∈Era\in E^{r}, fixed matrices F∈ℝp×rF\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times r} and R∈ℝr×pR\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times p} with F​R=IpFR=I_{p}, and coefficient row b=a​Rb=aR. The admitted labels satisfy

∥a−a​R​F∥∞≤ρ.\displaystyle\lVert a-aRF\rVert_{\infty}\leq\rho.

The coefficient matrix has a set of at least qp−vq^{p-v} approximate solutions in EpE^{p} at error ε\varepsilon. The state consists of the row count mm, input dimension pp, density loss vv, interpolation error ε\varepsilon, label error ρ\rho, and the two maps F,RF,R. Initially F=WF=W, R=W−1R=W^{-1}, m=dm=d, p=rp=r, v=uv=u, ρ=0\rho=0, and ε=ε0\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{0}, with the solution set in the proposition.

As long as ρ≤Δ/[4​(r+1)]\rho\leq\Delta/[4(r+1)], the number of labels with label error at most ρ\rho whose coefficient rows lie in a fixed subspace of dimension ℓ\ell is at most qℓq^{\ell}, by (3.4) applied to its image under multiplication by FF. In particular there are at most qpq^{p} choices for each row label. This counts labels even if a↦a​Ra\mapsto aR is not injective.

Apply Lemma 3.5 to a block of coefficient rows, and record J,IJ,I and the original labels of its hh selected rows. They determine BIB_{I}, hence TT and its specified right inverse UU. Replace F,RF,R by F′=T​FF^{\prime}=TF and R′=R​UR^{\prime}=RU. Then F′​R′=Ip′F^{\prime}R^{\prime}=I_{p^{\prime}}, and the new coefficient row for the same label is a​R′=b​UaR^{\prime}=bU. The new density loss is at most v−2​hv-2h. Every row of F′F^{\prime} is either an old row of FF or a row a​R​FaRF for a selected label. Thus, while all label errors are at most one, the entries of FF are bounded in terms of EE. In particular, ∥F∥≤C​K\lVert F\rVert\leq CK. The two error estimates in Lemma 3.5 therefore give

ε′≤C​(K+1)5​ε,ρ′≤ρ+C​(K+1)5​ε.\displaystyle\varepsilon^{\prime}\leq C(K+1)^{5}\varepsilon,\qquad\rho^{\prime}\leq\rho+C(K+1)^{5}\varepsilon.

For the second assertion, use the identity

a−a​R′​F′=a−a​R​F+(b−b​U​T)​F.\displaystyle a-aR^{\prime}F^{\prime}=a-aRF+(b-bUT)F.

The residual row b−b​U​Tb-bUT is bounded by the compression lemma, and multiplication by FF costs at most C​KCK. There is no multiplication by RR in this error estimate. Although RR initially is W−1W^{-1} and may have arbitrarily large norm, only F​R=IFR=I, the bounded entries of FF, and the residual in the displayed identity are used. The same facts hold at every child. This accounts for the uniformity in WW.

There are at most ⌈log2⁡K⌉+2\lceil\log_{2}K\rceil+2 reductions on a branch: one possible initial reduction, followed by division of the row set into two halves at each stage. Iterating the error bounds shows that both errors are at most eC​log2​(K+1)​ε0e^{C\log^{2}(K+1)}\varepsilon_{0}. Choose C3.2′C^{\prime}_{\ref{prop:approxcount}} large enough that

eC​log2​(K+1)​ε0≤min⁡{c3.5​K−4,Δ4​(K+1),1}.\displaystyle e^{C\log^{2}(K+1)}\varepsilon_{0}\leq\min\left\{c_{\ref{lem:compression}}K^{-4},\frac{\Delta}{4(K+1)},1\right\}.

Induction down each branch now verifies the error bounds and the hypotheses for the tube count at every node, uniformly in WW and the encoded matrix.

We bound the number of label arrays at a node with p≤L​mp\leq Lm by

exp⁡{C⁡[m​log⁡(m+1)+m⁡(v+1)]}.\displaystyle\exp\{C[m\log(m+1)+m(v+1)]\}. (3.5)

For p=0p=0 each row has at most one admitted label by (3.4); for m=1m=1 there are at most qLq^{L}. For m≥2m\geq 2, split the row indices into fixed blocks of sizes m1=⌊m/2⌋m_{1}=\lfloor m/2\rfloor and m2=⌈m/2⌉m_{2}=\lceil m/2\rceil. The parent’s approximate solution set satisfies the constraints of each block. Compress each block and record its selected data. For block ii the number of records is at most

2p+mi​qp​hi,0≤2​hi≤v.\displaystyle 2^{p+m_{i}}q^{ph_{i}},\qquad 0\leq 2h_{i}\leq v.

The reduced input dimension is at most L​miLm_{i}, and its density loss is at most v−2​hiv-2h_{i}. Applying the inductive bound and using p≤L​m≤3​L​mip\leq Lm\leq 3Lm_{i}, the logarithm of the count is at most

C′​m+max⁡∑i=12h1,h2⁡[C′​mi​hi+C​mi​log⁡(mi+1)+C​mi​(v−2​hi+1)].\displaystyle C^{\prime}m+\max_{h_{1},h_{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{2}\left[C^{\prime}m_{i}h_{i}+Cm_{i}\log(m_{i}+1)+Cm_{i}(v-2h_{i}+1)\right].

The choices of hih_{i} are included in the records of row sets; allowing an additional factor (m+1)2(m+1)^{2} also costs only O⁡(m)O(m). Since

m​log⁡(m+1)−∑imi​log⁡(mi+1)≥m​log⁡(4/3),\displaystyle m\log(m+1)-\sum_{i}m_{i}\log(m_{i}+1)\geq m\log(4/3),

choosing C​log⁡(4/3)≥C′C\log(4/3)\geq C^{\prime} and 2​C≥C′2C\geq C^{\prime} proves (3.5). Compression has changed the coordinate maps, but each child still counts the original labels assigned to its block. Joining the two arrays recovers the parent’s rows in their original order, and at the root recovers YY exactly.

If initially r>L​dr>Ld, compress the whole matrix once. Recording J,IJ,I and h≤u/2h\leq u/2 original rows costs at most 2r+d​qr​h2^{r+d}q^{rh}, whose logarithm is Oq​(K​(u+1))O_{q}(K(u+1)). The reduced matrix has at most L​dLd inputs and density loss at most u−2​hu-2h, so (3.5) applies. If r≤L​dr\leq Ld, apply it directly. Empty row or input sets have at most one possible matrix. This proves the proposition. ∎

We next prepare the choice of bases. A shifted projection estimate gives many prefixes with controlled conditioning, which we then complete by maximizing volume. The same projection estimate will also be used in the Fourier integral in Section 4.

Lemma 3.6.

Let bb be uniform on EsE^{s}, PP an orthogonal projection of rank h≥1h\geq 1, and v∈ℝsv\in\mathbb{R}^{s} deterministic. There are positive constants c3.6=c3.6​(E)c_{\ref{lem:projection}}=c_{\ref{lem:projection}}(E) and c3.6′=c3.6′​(E)c^{\prime}_{\ref{lem:projection}}=c^{\prime}_{\ref{lem:projection}}(E) such that

ℙ⁡(∥P⁡(b−v)∥22≤c3.6​h)≤2​e−c3.6′​h.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\lVert P(b-v)\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq c_{\ref{lem:projection}}h\right)\leq 2e^{-c^{\prime}_{\ref{lem:projection}}h}.
Proof.

Let σ2>0\sigma^{2}>0 be the variance of a random variable uniform on EE. The difference b−b′b-b^{\prime} of independent copies has independent, centered, bounded coordinates of variance 2​σ2>02\sigma^{2}>0. The Hanson–Wright inequality (Theorem 1.1 in [23]), using ∥P∥=1\lVert P\rVert=1 and ∥P∥HS2=h\lVert P\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}=h, gives ℙ⁡(∥P⁡(b−b′)∥22≤σ2​h)≤2​e−c​h\mathbb{P}\left(\lVert P(b-b^{\prime})\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\sigma^{2}h\right)\leq 2e^{-ch} for a constant c>0c>0 depending only on EE. Set c3.6=σ2/4c_{\ref{lem:projection}}=\sigma^{2}/4 and c3.6′=c/2c^{\prime}_{\ref{lem:projection}}=c/2. If both copies satisfy ∥P⁡(b−v)∥22≤c3.6​h\lVert P(b-v)\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq c_{\ref{lem:projection}}h, then their difference satisfies ∥P⁡(b−b′)∥22≤4​c3.6​h=σ2​h\lVert P(b-b^{\prime})\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 4c_{\ref{lem:projection}}h=\sigma^{2}h. Independence gives

ℙ(∥P(b−v)∥22≤c3.6h)≤2e−ch/2≤2e−c3.6′​h,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\lVert P(b-v)\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq c_{\ref{lem:projection}}h\right)\leq\sqrt{2}\,e^{-ch/2}\leq 2e^{-c^{\prime}_{\ref{lem:projection}}h},

as required. ∎

We shall need many bases rather than one basis with controlled conditioning. Their multiplicity permits the corresponding slab indicators to be averaged before integration. The dependence on the smallest singular value of an available basis is confined to OE​(u+1)O_{E}(u+1) completion directions, where uu denotes the density loss.

Lemma 3.7.

Fix a∈E∖{0}a\in E\setminus\{0\}. Suppose 𝒮⊂Er\mathcal{S}\subset E^{r} spans ℝr\mathbb{R}^{r}, contains a​𝟏ra\mathbf{1}_{r}, and |𝒮|≥qr−u|\mathcal{S}|\geq q^{r-u}, where u≥0u\geq 0. There is a constant C3.7>0C_{\ref{lem:densebases}}>0 depending only on EE such that, with

m=(r−1−⌈C3.7​(u+1)⌉)+,g=r−1−m,\displaystyle m=(r-1-\lceil C_{\ref{lem:densebases}}(u+1)\rceil)_{+},\qquad g=r-1-m,

at least e−C3.7​r​|𝒮|me^{-C_{\ref{lem:densebases}}r}|\mathcal{S}|^{m} ordered bases W=(a​𝟏r,x1,…,xr−1)W=(a\mathbf{1}_{r},x_{1},\ldots,x_{r-1}) with columns in 𝒮\mathcal{S} satisfy

supx∈𝒮∥W−1​x∥1≤C3.7​(r+1)4.\displaystyle\sup_{x\in\mathcal{S}}\lVert W^{-1}x\rVert_{1}\leq C_{\ref{lem:densebases}}(r+1)^{4}. (3.6)

If 𝒮\mathcal{S} contains a basis QQ with smin​(Q)≥ζs_{\min}(Q)\geq\zeta, 0<ζ≤10<\zeta\leq 1, the same bases can be chosen to satisfy

|detW|≥e−C3.7​r​log⁡(r+1)​ζg,g≤2​C3.7​(u+1).\displaystyle|\det W|\geq e^{-C_{\ref{lem:densebases}}r\log(r+1)}\zeta^{g},\qquad g\leq 2C_{\ref{lem:densebases}}(u+1). (3.7)
Proof.

We first produce many prefixes using an uncentered second moment matrix rather than a bound on every determinant. We then complete each prefix by maximal volume, which bounds all the remaining interpolation coordinates at once.

Let PP project onto 𝟏r⟂\mathbf{1}_{r}^{\perp}, let XX be uniform on 𝒮\mathcal{S}, and let Σ=𝔼⁡[(P​X)​(P​X)T]\Sigma=\mathbb{E}[(PX)(PX)^{T}] be its uncentered second moment matrix on that space of dimension r−1r-1. Use the constants c3.6,c3.6′c_{\ref{lem:projection}},c^{\prime}_{\ref{lem:projection}} from Lemma 3.6. If h≥1h\geq 1 eigenvalues of Σ\Sigma are less than c3.6/4c_{\ref{lem:projection}}/4, let Q0Q_{0} project onto their eigenspace. 4. Fourier estimates for concentration functions

We prove the averaging estimate used in the inversion of randomness argument. Rescaling and rounding an incompressible normal at scale TT produces an integer vector in a product set at scale N=Θ⁡(T−1)N=\Theta(T^{-1}). Theorem 4.2 shows that, throughout the range N≤qn​(n+1)−DN\leq q^{n}(n+1)^{-D}, only an e−ω⁡(n)e^{-\omega(n)} proportion of these vectors can have concentration at least L4.2/NL_{\ref{thm:averaging}}/N. The constant in the exponent can be chosen arbitrarily large without changing this threshold.

We use the admissible product sets from Section 4 in [32]. Their three properties enter separately: the coordinate ranges allow averaging over the coefficients; a positive proportion of coordinates stay away from zero and control the lowest frequencies; and the product bound |𝒜|≤(K​N)n|\mathcal{A}|\leq(KN)^{n} converts an exceptional proportion into a count of rounded vectors. The individual cardinalities |Ai||A_{i}| need not be Θ⁡(N)\Theta(N).

Definition 4.1.

For positive integers N,nN,n, K≥1K\geq 1, and δ∈(0,1]\delta\in(0,1], a product 𝒜=∏i=1nAi⊂ℤn\mathcal{A}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}\subset\mathbb{Z}^{n} is admissible with parameters (N,n,K,δ)(N,n,K,\delta) if:

  1. (i)

    Ai=−AiA_{i}=-A_{i};

  2. (ii)

    for i>δ​ni>\delta n, AiA_{i} is an integer interval of size at least 2​N+12N+1;

  3. (iii)

    for i≤δ​ni\leq\delta n, AiA_{i} is the union of two integer intervals, each of size at least NN, and Ai∩[−N,N]=∅A_{i}\cap[-N,N]=\emptyset;

  4. (iv)

    ∏i|Ai|≤(K​N)n\prod_{i}|A_{i}|\leq(KN)^{n} and maxa∈Ai⁡|a|<n​N\max_{a\in A_{i}}|a|<nN for every ii.

Theorem 4.2.

Let E⊂ℝE\subset\mathbb{R} be a fixed set of q≥2q\geq 2 points. For fixed δ∈(0,1]\delta\in(0,1] and K≥1K\geq 1, there is L4.2=L4.2​(E,δ,K)>0L_{\ref{thm:averaging}}=L_{\ref{thm:averaging}}(E,\delta,K)>0 independent of M,DM,D such that for every M≥1M\geq 1 and D>1D>1, the following holds for all n≥n4.2​(E,δ,K,M,D)n\geq n_{\ref{thm:averaging}}(E,\delta,K,M,D) and all integers

1≤N≤qn​(n+1)−D:\displaystyle 1\leq N\leq q^{n}(n+1)^{-D}:

a uniform vector XX on any set admissible with parameters (N,n,K,δ)(N,n,K,\delta) satisfies

ℙX​(ℒb​(∑i=1nbi​Xi,n)≥L4.2N)≤e−M​n.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{X}\left(\mathcal{L}_{b}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}X_{i},\sqrt{n}\right)\geq\frac{L_{\ref{thm:averaging}}}{N}\right)\leq e^{-Mn}. (4.1)

The variables bib_{i} are independent and uniformly distributed on EE, and are independent of XX; ℒb\mathcal{L}_{b} denotes concentration with respect to the variables bib_{i}, with the coefficients fixed.

Equivalently, at most e−M​n​|𝒜|e^{-Mn}|\mathcal{A}| integer vectors in 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfy the concentration condition in (4.1). Related averaging estimates appear in Corollary 4.3 in [32] and in the work of Jain, Sah and Sawhney [10]. For uniform finite supports, the latter applies in a range separated from qnq^{n} by a fixed exponential factor. Here the range is only a polynomial factor below qnq^{n}.

For fixed coefficients, translating EE by one of its elements only translates the scalar linear form. Its concentration function is unchanged. We therefore assume 0∈E0\in E throughout the proof of the averaging theorem. This does not translate the random matrix in Theorem 1.1.

We pass to continuous coefficients to turn the count of integer vectors into volume and integral estimates suited to Fourier analysis. Adding independent bounded perturbations preserves concentration at the n\sqrt{n} scale up to constant factors, with probability bounded below. The construction and comparison are given in the proof below. For the continuous estimate, let Z1,…,ZnZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{n} be independent. For i>⌊δ​n⌋i>\lfloor\delta n\rfloor, the variable ZiZ_{i} is uniform on a bounded interval IiI_{i}; for i≤⌊δ​n⌋i\leq\lfloor\delta n\rfloor, it is uniform on the union IiI_{i} of two disjoint bounded intervals. Every component interval has length at least NN. We assume

Ii⊂[−2nN,2nN],∏i=1n|Ii|≤(KN)n,Ii∩(−N/2,N/2)=∅(i≤⌊δn⌋),\displaystyle I_{i}\subset[-2nN,2nN],\qquad\prod_{i=1}^{n}|I_{i}|\leq(KN)^{n},\qquad I_{i}\cap(-N/2,N/2)=\emptyset\quad(i\leq\lfloor\delta n\rfloor),

where |Ii||I_{i}| denotes Lebesgue measure. Write μi\mu_{i} for the density of ZiZ_{i}.

Outside the union of the two exceptional events,

The union bound gives exceptional probability at most 2​e−(M+1)​n≤e−M​n2e^{-(M+1)n}\leq e^{-Mn}. This proves the proposition. ∎

4.2. High moments and the far frequency estimate

Write 𝔪={θ:|θ|>n2/N}\mathfrak{m}=\{\theta:|\theta|>n^{2}/N\}. For r≥1r\geq 1, define Hr={z∈ℝr:∑jzj=0}H_{r}=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{r}:\sum_{j}z_{j}=0\}, with the measure obtained by eliminating one coordinate. In the chart zr=−∑j<rzjz_{r}=-\sum_{j<r}z_{j}, this is dz1⋯dzr−1dz_{1}\cdots dz_{r-1}. The measure is invariant under coordinate permutations, and an integral in dimension zero equals one.

The following lemma converts the supremum bound into a high moment. The moment is taken before absolute values are introduced into the Fourier integral, so the relations between the frequencies are retained.

Lemma 4.7.

For each coefficient density μi\mu_{i}, there is a probability density νi\nu_{i} such that

μi≤2νi,|ν^i(t)|≤e−a​N2​t2(t∈ℝ),\displaystyle\mu_{i}\leq 2\nu_{i},\qquad|\widehat{\nu}_{i}(t)|\leq e^{-aN^{2}t^{2}}\quad(t\in\mathbb{R}), (4.3)

Ki​(θ)=q−k​∑v∈Ekν^i​(−⟨v,θ⟩).\displaystyle K_{i}(\theta)=q^{-k}\sum_{v\in E^{k}}\widehat{\nu}_{i}(-\langle v,\theta\rangle).

ℙZ​(∥RZ∥∞>1N​n)≤2n​C4.7k​Nk+1​n(k−1)/2​∫Hk∩𝔪k∏j=1kωn​(θj)​∏i=1n|Ki​(θ)|​𝑑θ.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{Z}\left(\lVert R_{Z}\rVert_{\infty}>\frac{1}{N\sqrt{n}}\right)\leq 2^{n}C_{\ref{lem:moment}}^{k}N^{k+1}n^{(k-1)/2}\int_{H_{k}\cap\mathfrak{m}^{k}}\prod_{j=1}^{k}\omega_{n}(\theta_{j})\prod_{i=1}^{n}|K_{i}(\theta)|\,d\theta. (4.4)
Proof.

Conjugate symmetry makes RzR_{z} real valued. Differentiation under the integrable Gaussian gives

∥Rz′∥∞≤∫ℝ2​π​|θ|​e−2​π2​β2​n​θ2​𝑑θ=1π​β2​n.\displaystyle\lVert R^{\prime}_{z}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}}2\pi|\theta|e^{-2\pi^{2}\beta^{2}n\theta^{2}}\,d\theta=\frac{1}{\pi\beta^{2}n}.

For gz=𝟏𝔪​ωn​Φzg_{z}=\mathbf{1}_{\mathfrak{m}}\omega_{n}\Phi_{z}, we have gz∈L1∩L2g_{z}\in L^{1}\cap L^{2} and gz​(−θ)=gz​(θ)¯g_{z}(-\theta)=\overline{g_{z}(\theta)}. Writing k=2​ℓk=2\ell, Plancherel applied to RzℓR_{z}^{\ell} and the convolution of ℓ\ell copies of gzg_{z} gives

∫ℝRz​(x)k​𝑑x=gz∗k​(0)=∫Hk∩𝔪k∏j=1kωn​(θj)​∏i=1n∏j=1kφ⁡(zi​θj)​𝑑θ.\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}R_{z}(x)^{k}\,dx=g_{z}^{*k}(0)=\int_{H_{k}\cap\mathfrak{m}^{k}}\prod_{j=1}^{k}\omega_{n}(\theta_{j})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=1}^{k}\varphi(z_{i}\theta_{j})\,d\theta.

The constraint ∑jθj=0\sum_{j}\theta_{j}=0 accounts for HkH_{k}; convolution uses exactly its measure defined by eliminating one coordinate, with no additional normalizing factor. We now introduce auxiliary densities solely to average this nonnegative spatial moment. We construct the densities νi\nu_{i} as follows.

On an interval of length ℓ\ell, convolve the uniform density on the concentric interval of length 3​ℓ/23\ell/2 with a centered Gaussian of standard deviation ℓ/16\ell/16. On the original interval this density is at least

23​ℓ​ℙ​(|G|≤ℓ/4)≥12​ℓ.\displaystyle\frac{2}{3\ell}\mathbb{P}\left(|G|\leq\ell/4\right)\geq\frac{1}{2\ell}.

Its Fourier transform has modulus at most e−a​ℓ2​t2e^{-a\ell^{2}t^{2}}. For two intervals, mix these densities with the original interval weights. This proves (4.3).

Since kk is even, z↦∫ℝRz​(x)k​𝑑xz\mapsto\int_{\mathbb{R}}R_{z}(x)^{k}\,dx is nonnegative. Hence

by (4.3). Let Z~i\widetilde{Z}_{i} be independent with densities νi\nu_{i}. Expanding the characteristic functions before integrating in Z~i\widetilde{Z}_{i} gives

𝔼​∏j=1kφ⁡(Z~i​θj)=q−k​∑(v1,…,vk)∈Ek𝔼​e2​π​i​Z~i​(v1​θ1+⋯+vk​θk)=q−k​∑v∈Ekν^i​(−⟨v,θ⟩)=:Ki​(θ).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\prod_{j=1}^{k}\varphi(\widetilde{Z}_{i}\theta_{j})=q^{-k}\sum_{(v_{1},\ldots,v_{k})\in E^{k}}\mathbb{E}e^{2\pi i\widetilde{Z}_{i}(v_{1}\theta_{1}+\cdots+v_{k}\theta_{k})}=q^{-k}\sum_{v\in E^{k}}\widehat{\nu}_{i}(-\langle v,\theta\rangle)=:K_{i}(\theta).

The Gaussian product is integrable on HkH_{k}, so Fubini justifies these exchanges before absolute values are taken. Finally, at λ=(N​n)−1\lambda=(N\sqrt{n})^{-1},

1n​λk+1=Nk+1​n(k−1)/2.\displaystyle\frac{1}{n\lambda^{k+1}}=N^{k+1}n^{(k-1)/2}.

Substitution in the preceding supremum estimate gives (4.4). ∎

We now express the kernel bounds in terms of approximate relations. With aa as in (4.3), set

R=3​k​log⁡q/a,V⁡(θ)={v∈Ek:|⟨v,θ⟩|≤R/N}.\displaystyle R=\sqrt{3k\log q/a},\qquad V(\theta)=\{v\in E^{k}:|\langle v,\theta\rangle|\leq R/N\}.

Thus V⁡(θ)V(\theta) is the set of approximate relation vectors associated with θ\theta, and |V⁡(θ)||V(\theta)| counts these vectors without any requirement of linear independence.

For a uniform vector b∈Ekb\in E^{k},

q−k​|V⁡(θ)|=ℙb​(|⟨b,θ⟩|≤R/N).\displaystyle q^{-k}|V(\theta)|=\mathbb{P}_{b}\left(|\langle b,\theta\rangle|\leq R/N\right).

Thus the normalized number of relations is a small ball probability. Equation (4.3) and e−a​R2=q−3​ke^{-aR^{2}}=q^{-3k} give

|Ki​(θ)|≤q−k​∑v∈V⁡(θ)e−a​N2​(⟨v,θ⟩)2+q−3​k≤q−k​|V⁡(θ)|+q−3​k.\displaystyle|K_{i}(\theta)|\leq q^{-k}\sum_{v\in V(\theta)}e^{-aN^{2}(\langle v,\theta\rangle)^{2}}+q^{-3k}\leq q^{-k}|V(\theta)|+q^{-3k}. (4.5)

We retain both bounds: the cardinality controls most factors, while the Gaussian weights will be used to integrate the remaining factors. The task is to estimate the frequency regions on which there are many relations. This combination of counting and integration is analogous to using small ball estimates with a union bound over a structured net; see Section 5.2 in [21]. Here we count spaces of approximate relations in EkE^{k} and integrate over the associated frequency regions.

The next lemma selects such a space without requiring a lower bound on every nonzero determinant with entries in EE.

We use two auxiliary estimates in the part of the proof with bounded density loss. The first integrates the Gaussian average that occurs in (4.5); the second localizes dense sets of relations and makes sufficiently accurate interpolation exact.

Lemma 4.9.

For bounded density loss, scalar anticoncentration confines the coefficients that can be large. There are then only finitely many interpolation problems of bounded size in ErE^{r}. Small inner products then localize a frequency, while sufficiently accurate approximate labels become exact labels. Neither assertion requires a determinant bound in a growing dimension.

Lemma 4.10.

Multiply this bound for one slab set by the total weight (4.9) and by the uniform kernel bound (1+ε)n​q−n⁡(d+t)(1+\varepsilon)^{n}q^{-n(d+t)} from (4.6). After inserting the moment normalization and cancelling the powers of NN as in the case of bounded density loss, we obtain

𝒯d,t≤\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{d,t}\leq{} [2​q2​(1+ε)]n​Ck​(2​R)r−1​n(r−1)/2​e−(d+2)​Δn−n​t​log⁡q\displaystyle[2q^{2}(1+\varepsilon)]^{n}C^{k}(2R)^{r-1}n^{(r-1)/2}\,e^{-(d+2)\Delta_{n}-nt\log q}
⋅exp⁡{C​k​(t+2)+C​k​log⁡(k+1)+C⁡(t+2)​log2⁡(k+1)}.\displaystyle\quad\cdot\exp\{Ck(t+2)+Ck\log(k+1)+C(t+2)\log^{2}(k+1)\}.

The term d​log⁡(k+1)d\log(k+1) has been included in C​k​log⁡(k+1)Ck\log(k+1). With k=A​n/log⁡(n+1)+O⁡(1)k=An/\log(n+1)+O(1) and R=C​kR=C\sqrt{k}, this gives

log⁡𝒯d,t≤C⁡(A+1)​n+C​k​(t+2)+C⁡(t+2)​log2⁡(k+1)−n​t​log​q.\displaystyle\log\mathcal{T}_{d,t}\leq C(A+1)n+Ck(t+2)+C(t+2)\log^{2}(k+1)-nt\log q. (4.11)

All these bounds are uniform in d,td,t and the permitted NN.

Choice of parameters and summation. All constants in the counting and geometric estimates, including C4.8C_{\ref{lem:relations}}, were fixed using only the support. Choose AA so that

A⁡(D−1)/2>M+log⁡(2​q2)+10.\displaystyle A(D-1)/2>M+\log(2q^{2})+10.

It follows that 𝒯d,t≤e−(M+4)​n\mathcal{T}_{d,t}\leq e^{-(M+4)n} throughout this range, after increasing n4.6​(E,M,D)n_{\ref{prop:far}}(E,M,D).

For t≤Tt\leq T, the errors in (4.8) are uniform over d,t,Nd,t,N. Indeed, k​log⁡(n/(2​k))=o⁡(n)k\log(n/(2k))=o(n), and any constant depending only on E,TE,T multiplied by kk is o⁡(n)o(n). The choice of AA therefore gives 𝒯d,t≤e−(M+4)​n\mathcal{T}_{d,t}\leq e^{-(M+4)n} in this range as well.

5. Proof of the main theorem

We combine Theorem 4.2 with the inversion of randomness argument in Section 5 in [32] and the structured estimate of Jain, Sah and Sawhney [10]. The scale weighting in Proposition 5.3 below preserves the polynomial remainder. Throughout this section, ξ\xi is uniform on SS, q=|S|≥2q=|S|\geq 2, and 𝝃=(ξ1,…,ξn)\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n}) has independent coordinates with this law.

For δ∈(0,1/4]\delta\in(0,1/4] and ν∈(0,1/2]\nu\in(0,1/2], let Comp⁡(δ,ν)\operatorname{Comp}(\delta,\nu) be the unit vectors within Euclidean distance ν\nu of a vector supported on at most ⌊δ​n⌋\lfloor\delta n\rfloor coordinates, and let Incomp⁡(δ,ν)\operatorname{Incomp}(\delta,\nu) be its complement in the unit sphere, as in [21]. We need the following consequence of the structured estimate.

Lemma 5.1.

There are δ5.1∈(0,1/4]\delta_{\ref{lem:structured}}\in(0,1/4], ν5.1∈(0,1/2]\nu_{\ref{lem:structured}}\in(0,1/2] and η5.1>0\eta_{\ref{lem:structured}}>0 depending only on SS such that, with δ=δ5.1\delta=\delta_{\ref{lem:structured}} and ν=ν5.1\nu=\nu_{\ref{lem:structured}}, for n≥n5.1​(S)n\geq n_{\ref{lem:structured}}(S) and 0≤t≤10\leq t\leq 1,

ℙ⁡(infx∈Comp⁡(δ,ν)∥Mn​x∥2≤t)≤12​an​(S)+(t+q−n)​e−η5.1​n.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\inf_{x\in\operatorname{Comp}(\delta,\nu)}\lVert M_{n}x\rVert_{2}\leq t\right)\leq\tfrac{1}{2}a_{n}(S)+(t+q^{-n})e^{-\eta_{\ref{lem:structured}}n}. (5.1)
Proof.

Apply the estimate for almost constant vectors in [10], and denote its parameters by δ0,ρ0\delta_{0},\rho_{0}. If x∈Comp⁡(δ,ν)x\in\operatorname{Comp}(\delta,\nu), at most (δ+ν2/ρ02)​n(\delta+\nu^{2}/\rho_{0}^{2})n coordinates have absolute value greater than ρ0/n\rho_{0}/\sqrt{n}. Choose δ≤δ0/2\delta\leq\delta_{0}/2 and ν2≤δ0​ρ02/2\nu^{2}\leq\delta_{0}\rho_{0}^{2}/2. Then xx belongs to the class in that theorem, with common value zero. Its elementary contribution is an​(S)/2a_{n}(S)/2, giving (5.1). ∎

For L≥1L\geq 1 and a unit vector xx, define

τ⁡(x)=sup{u∈(0,1]:ℒξ​(⟨𝝃,x⟩,u)>L​u}.\displaystyle\tau(x)=\sup\{u\in(0,1]:\mathcal{L}_{\xi}(\langle\boldsymbol{\xi},x\rangle,u)>Lu\}.

We collect the rounding and geometric inputs into one statement at each concentration scale. Random rounding appears in the work of Klartag and Livshyts [12], Livshyts [17], and Livshyts, Tikhomirov and Vershynin [16]. Below we adapt the argument of Lemma 5.3 in [32] to the fixed finite support SS.

Lemma 5.2.

Fix δ∈(0,1/4]\delta\in(0,1/4] and ν∈(0,1/2]\nu\in(0,1/2]. There are constants L5.2,C5.2≥1L_{\ref{lem:roundednet}},C_{\ref{lem:roundednet}}\geq 1 depending only on S,δ,νS,\delta,\nu such that, with L=L5.2L=L_{\ref{lem:roundednet}}, for every M≥1M\geq 1, D>1D>1 and n≥n5.2​(S,δ,ν,M,D)n\geq n_{\ref{lem:roundednet}}(S,\delta,\nu,M,D), the following hold. For every x∈Incomp⁡(δ,ν)x\in\operatorname{Incomp}(\delta,\nu), we have q−n/L≤τ⁡(x)≤ν/nq^{-n}/L\leq\tau(x)\leq\nu/\sqrt{n} and

ℒξ​(⟨𝝃,x⟩,u)≤L​u​(u≥τ⁡(x)),ℒξ​(⟨𝝃,x⟩,τ⁡(x))≥L​τ​(x).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\xi}(\langle\boldsymbol{\xi},x\rangle,u)\leq Lu\ (u\geq\tau(x)),\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\xi}(\langle\boldsymbol{\xi},x\rangle,\tau(x))\geq L\tau(x). (5.2)

If 0<T≤ν/40<T\leq\nu/4 and N=⌊ν/T⌋−1≤qn​(n+1)−DN=\lfloor\nu/T\rfloor-1\leq q^{n}(n+1)^{-D}, there is a deterministic set 𝒩T⊂ℤn\mathcal{N}_{T}\subset\mathbb{Z}^{n} with

|𝒩T|≤e−M​n(C5.2N)n,ℙξ(|⟨𝝃,y⟩|≤a)≤C5.2Ta/n(y∈𝒩T,a≥n).\displaystyle|\mathcal{N}_{T}|\leq e^{-Mn}(C_{\ref{lem:roundednet}}N)^{n},\qquad\mathbb{P}_{\xi}\left(|\langle\boldsymbol{\xi},y\rangle|\leq a\right)\leq C_{\ref{lem:roundednet}}Ta/\sqrt{n}\quad(y\in\mathcal{N}_{T},\ a\geq\sqrt{n}). (5.3)

Every x∈Incomp⁡(δ,ν)x\in\operatorname{Incomp}(\delta,\nu) with T/2<τ⁡(x)≤TT/2<\tau(x)\leq T admits y∈𝒩Ty\in\mathcal{N}_{T} such that, for e=y−n​x/τ⁡(x)e=y-\sqrt{n}\,x/\tau(x),

∥e∥∞≤1,|⟨𝟏n,e⟩|≤C5.2​n.\displaystyle\lVert e\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1,\qquad|\langle\mathbf{1}_{n},e\rangle|\leq C_{\ref{lem:roundednet}}\sqrt{n}. (5.4)
Proof.

As in Lemma 5.1 in [32], the ⌊δ​n⌋\lfloor\delta n\rfloor largest coordinates of an incompressible vector have absolute value greater than ν/n\nu/\sqrt{n}. Lemma 3.3 and interval covering therefore give ℒξ(⟨𝝃,x⟩,u)≤C(n−1/2+u)\mathcal{L}_{\xi}(\langle\boldsymbol{\xi},x\rangle,u)\leq C(n^{-1/2}+u). Taking LL large enough yields the upper bound on τ\tau. An atom of mass at least q−nq^{-n} gives the lower bound. The two endpoint estimates follow from the definition, monotonicity and right continuity of the concentration function.

Set y0=n​x/τ⁡(x)y^{0}=\sqrt{n}\,x/\tau(x). Lemma 5.3 in [32] extends to the present coefficients with constants depending only on SS. Indeed, its independent unbiased rounding errors satisfy

|ei|≤1,𝔼e​|⟨b,e⟩|2≤R2​n/4​(b∈Sn),𝔼e​|⟨𝟏n,e⟩|2≤n/4,R=maxb∈S⁡|b|.\displaystyle|e_{i}|\leq 1,\qquad\mathbb{E}_{e}|\langle b,e\rangle|^{2}\leq R^{2}n/4\ (b\in S^{n}),\qquad\mathbb{E}_{e}|\langle\mathbf{1}_{n},e\rangle|^{2}\leq n/4,\quad R=\max_{b\in S}|b|.

These replace the variance bounds for Bernoulli configurations in the cited proof, with its configuration weights replaced by the product law on SnS^{n}. The dyadic shell argument for the upper bound and the mass retention argument for the lower bound then give a rounding satisfying (5.4) and

ℙξ​(|⟨𝝃,y⟩|≤a)≤CS​L​T​a/n(a≥n),ℒξ​(⟨𝝃,y⟩,n)≥cS​L​τ​(x)>cS​L​T/2.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\xi}\left(|\langle\boldsymbol{\xi},y\rangle|\leq a\right)\leq C_{S}LTa/\sqrt{n}\quad(a\geq\sqrt{n}),\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\xi}(\langle\boldsymbol{\xi},y\rangle,\sqrt{n})\geq c_{S}L\tau(x)>c_{S}LT/2.

The sum error is controlled by the last variance bound, exactly as in that lemma.

By Corollary 5.5 and Lemma 5.6 in [32], these rounded vectors lie in at most C0nC_{0}^{n} coordinate permutations of one product set admissible with parameters (N,n,K,δ)(N,n,K,\delta), where K=K⁡(δ,ν)K=K(\delta,\nu) and C0C_{0} is universal. The geometric construction in the proof of Lemma 5.4 there uses only incompressibility and the error bound ∥y−n​x/s∥∞≤1\lVert y-\sqrt{n}\,x/s\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1, for T/2<s≤TT/2<s\leq T, so it applies independently of the coefficient law. Also ν/2≤N​T≤ν\nu/2\leq NT\leq\nu. Write Lav=L4.2​(S,δ,K)L_{\mathrm{av}}=L_{\ref{thm:averaging}}(S,\delta,K), and choose L≥4​Lav/(cS​ν)L\geq 4L_{\mathrm{av}}/(c_{S}\nu), in addition to the earlier lower bound. Then the rounded vector has concentration at least Lav/NL_{\mathrm{av}}/N. Let 𝒩T\mathcal{N}_{T} consist of the vectors in these permuted sets with this concentration and the preceding small ball upper bound. Theorem 4.2 gives |𝒩T|≤C0n​e−M​n​(K​N)n|\mathcal{N}_{T}|\leq C_{0}^{n}e^{-Mn}(KN)^{n}. Enlarge C5.2C_{\ref{lem:roundednet}} to include C0​KC_{0}K, CS​LC_{S}L and the sum error constant. All choices precede M,DM,D. ∎

Proposition 5.3.

Fix δ∈(0,1/4]\delta\in(0,1/4] and ν∈(0,1/2]\nu\in(0,1/2], and use the threshold τ\tau from Lemma 5.2. Write Cj=colj⁡(Mn)C_{j}=\operatorname{col}_{j}(M_{n}), and choose a unit normal YjY_{j} to the other columns, measurably with respect to those columns. There is C5.3>0C_{\ref{prop:normal}}>0 depending only on S,δ,νS,\delta,\nu such that for every D>1D>1 and B>0B>0 there is C5.3′>0C^{\prime}_{\ref{prop:normal}}>0 depending also on D,BD,B for which, for n≥n5.3​(S,δ,ν,D,B)n\geq n_{\ref{prop:normal}}(S,\delta,\nu,D,B) and h≥0h\geq 0,

𝔼[τ(Yj)𝟏{Yj∈Incomp(δ,ν)}]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(Y_{j})\mathbf{1}_{\{Y_{j}\in\operatorname{Incomp}(\delta,\nu)\}}\right] ≤C5.3′​(n+1)D​q−n+e−B​n,\displaystyle\leq C^{\prime}_{\ref{prop:normal}}(n+1)^{D}q^{-n}+e^{-Bn},
ℙ⁡(Yj∈Incomp⁡(δ,ν),|⟨Cj,Yj⟩|≤h)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(Y_{j}\in\operatorname{Incomp}(\delta,\nu),\ |\langle C_{j},Y_{j}\rangle|\leq h\right) ≤C5.3​h+C5.3′​(n+1)D​q−n+C5.3​e−B​n.\displaystyle\leq C_{\ref{prop:normal}}h+C^{\prime}_{\ref{prop:normal}}(n+1)^{D}q^{-n}+C_{\ref{prop:normal}}e^{-Bn}. (5.5)
Proof.

Write Y=YjY=Y_{j}, let M−jM_{-j} be the matrix with column jj deleted, and set ℱj=σ(Ci:i≠j)\mathcal{F}_{j}=\sigma(C_{i}:i\neq j). The finite support permits a measurable choice of YY even if the other columns are linearly dependent. Conditional on ℱj\mathcal{F}_{j}, CjC_{j} retains its product law. Thus, on {Y∈Incomp}\{Y\in\operatorname{Incomp}\},

ℙ⁡(|⟨Cj,Y⟩|≤h∣ℱj)≤L​max⁡{h,τ⁡(Y)}≤L​h+L​τ​(Y),\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(|\langle C_{j},Y\rangle|\leq h\mid\mathcal{F}_{j}\right)\leq L\max\{h,\tau(Y)\}\leq Lh+L\tau(Y),

where L=L5.2L=L_{\ref{lem:roundednet}}. It suffices to prove the expectation bound.

Set μ=𝔼​ξ\mu=\mathbb{E}\xi and Z−j=M−j−μ​𝟏n​𝟏n−1TZ_{-j}=M_{-j}-\mu\mathbf{1}_{n}\mathbf{1}_{n-1}^{T}. Lemma 3.4 in [32], applied to the centered square matrix, gives K=K⁡(S,B)K=K(S,B) such that

ℙ(𝒢jc)≤e−(B+3)​n,𝒢j={∥Z−j∥≤Kn}.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}_{j}^{c})\leq e^{-(B+3)n},\qquad\mathcal{G}_{j}=\{\lVert Z_{-j}\rVert\leq K\sqrt{n}\}. (5.6)

Set N∗=⌊qn​(n+1)−D⌋N_{*}=\lfloor q^{n}(n+1)^{-D}\rfloor, T∗=ν/(N∗+1)T_{*}=\nu/(N_{*}+1), and Tℓ=2−ℓ​ν/nT_{\ell}=2^{-\ell}\nu/\sqrt{n}. For n≥n5.3​(S,δ,ν,D,B)n\geq n_{\ref{prop:normal}}(S,\delta,\nu,D,B), we have N∗≥1N_{*}\geq 1 and T0≤ν/4T_{0}\leq\nu/4. The scales from T0T_{0} down to the last Tℓ≥T∗T_{\ell}\geq T_{*} give Oq​(n)O_{q}(n) levels 𝒟T={x∈Incomp:T/2<τ⁡(x)≤T}\mathcal{D}_{T}=\{x\in\operatorname{Incomp}:T/2<\tau(x)\leq T\}. They cover the incompressible event apart from scales below T∗T_{*}, whose contribution to the expectation is at most T∗<ν​(n+1)D​q−nT_{*}<\nu(n+1)^{D}q^{-n}. Each associated N=⌊ν/T⌋−1N=\lfloor\nu/T\rfloor-1 satisfies 1≤N≤N∗1\leq N\leq N_{*} and ν/2≤N​T≤ν\nu/2\leq NT\leq\nu.

Fix one such level and take 𝒩T\mathcal{N}_{T} from Lemma 5.2, with exponent MM to be chosen below. On {Y=x∈𝒟T}∩𝒢j\{Y=x\in\mathcal{D}_{T}\}\cap\mathcal{G}_{j}, let y0=n​x/τ⁡(x)y^{0}=\sqrt{n}\,x/\tau(x) and take its rounding y∈𝒩Ty\in\mathcal{N}_{T}. Since M−jT​y0=0M_{-j}^{T}y^{0}=0, (5.4) yields

∥M−jT​y∥2≤K​n​∥y−y0∥2+|μ|​n−1​|⟨𝟏n,y−y0⟩|≤CB​n.\displaystyle\lVert M_{-j}^{T}y\rVert_{2}\leq K\sqrt{n}\,\lVert y-y^{0}\rVert_{2}+|\mu|\sqrt{n-1}\,|\langle\mathbf{1}_{n},y-y^{0}\rangle|\leq C_{B}n.

ℙ⁡(∥M−jT​y∥2≤CB​n)≤(CB​T)n−1.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\lVert M_{-j}^{T}y\rVert_{2}\leq C_{B}n\right)\leq(C_{B}T)^{n-1}.

This estimate is applied without conditioning on 𝒢j\mathcal{G}_{j}. The union bound and (5.3) therefore imply

where CB′C_{B}^{\prime} depends only on S,δ,ν,BS,\delta,\nu,B. Weighting by τ⁡(Y)≤T\tau(Y)\leq T removes the factor T−1T^{-1}:

𝔼[τ(Y)𝟏{Y∈𝒟T}∩𝒢j]≤e−(M−CB′)​n.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\tau(Y)\mathbf{1}_{\{Y\in\mathcal{D}_{T}\}\cap\mathcal{G}_{j}}\right]\leq e^{-(M-C_{B}^{\prime})n}.

Equivalently, the powers of the scale cancel as Nn​Tn−1​T=(N​T)nN^{n}T^{n-1}T=(NT)^{n}. Choose M>CB′+B+5M>C_{B}^{\prime}+B+5, and then choose n5.3n_{\ref{prop:normal}} to include the threshold in Lemma 5.2 and the preceding scale restrictions. Summing over the Oq​(n)O_{q}(n) levels and using τ≤1\tau\leq 1 on 𝒢jc\mathcal{G}_{j}^{c} proves the expectation bound.
