Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Fix δ,ν\delta,\nu from Lemma 5.1, take D=1+εD=1+\varepsilon and B>log⁡q+1B>\log q+1, and assume n≥max⁡{2/δ,n5.1​(S),n5.3​(S,δ,ν,D,B)}n\geq\max\{2/\delta,n_{\ref{lem:structured}}(S),n_{\ref{prop:normal}}(S,\delta,\nu,D,B)\}. For 0≤z≤ν0\leq z\leq\nu, let

𝒞z={infx∈Comp⁡(δ,ν)∥Mnx∥2≤z/n}∪{infy∈Comp⁡(δ,ν)∥MnTy∥2≤z/ν}.\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{z}=\left\{\inf_{x\in\operatorname{Comp}(\delta,\nu)}\lVert M_{n}x\rVert_{2}\leq z/\sqrt{n}\right\}\cup\left\{\inf_{y\in\operatorname{Comp}(\delta,\nu)}\lVert M_{n}^{T}y\rVert_{2}\leq z/\nu\right\}.

Applying (5.1) to the matrix and its transpose gives

ℙ⁡(𝒞z)≤an​(S)+(z/n+z/ν+2​q−n)​e−η5.1​n.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}_{z})\leq a_{n}(S)+(z/\sqrt{n}+z/\nu+2q^{-n})e^{-\eta_{\ref{lem:structured}}n}.

On {sn(Mn)≤z/n}∩𝒞zc\{s_{n}(M_{n})\leq z/\sqrt{n}\}\cap\mathcal{C}_{z}^{c}, a minimizing unit vector xx is incompressible. Each of its m=⌊δ​n⌋m=\lfloor\delta n\rfloor largest coordinates has absolute value greater than ν/n\nu/\sqrt{n}, since the squared norm outside them exceeds ν2\nu^{2}. For each corresponding index jj, orthogonality gives

|xj|​|⟨Cj,Yj⟩|=|⟨Mn​x,Yj⟩|≤z/n.\displaystyle|x_{j}|\,|\langle C_{j},Y_{j}\rangle|=|\langle M_{n}x,Y_{j}\rangle|\leq z/\sqrt{n}.

Hence |⟨Cj,Yj⟩|≤z/ν|\langle C_{j},Y_{j}\rangle|\leq z/\nu and ∥MnT​Yj∥2≤z/ν\lVert M_{n}^{T}Y_{j}\rVert_{2}\leq z/\nu; exclusion of 𝒞z\mathcal{C}_{z} forces Yj∈IncompY_{j}\in\operatorname{Incomp}. The resulting pointwise column average is

𝟏{sn(Mn)≤z/n}∩𝒞zc≤1m∑j=1n𝟏{Yj∈Incomp,|⟨Cj,Yj⟩|≤z/ν}.\displaystyle\mathbf{1}_{\{s_{n}(M_{n})\leq z/\sqrt{n}\}\cap\mathcal{C}_{z}^{c}}\leq\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}_{\{Y_{j}\in\operatorname{Incomp},\ |\langle C_{j},Y_{j}\rangle|\leq z/\nu\}}.

Since m≥δ​n/2m\geq\delta n/2, Proposition 5.3 bounds its expectation by (2/δ)​(C​z/ν+C′​(n+1)D​q−n+C​e−B​n)(2/\delta)(Cz/\nu+C^{\prime}(n+1)^{D}q^{-n}+Ce^{-Bn}). Adding the structured contribution, and absorbing e−B​n+q−n​e−η5.1​ne^{-Bn}+q^{-n}e^{-\eta_{\ref{lem:structured}}n} into C′​n1+ε​q−nC^{\prime}n^{1+\varepsilon}q^{-n}, proves (1.2) in this range. The coefficient of zz depends only on SS, since δ,ν,L\delta,\nu,L were fixed before D,BD,B. Increase CC to cover z>νz>\nu and C′C^{\prime} to cover the finitely many remaining dimensions. ∎

To deduce Corollary 1.2, we also need to compare the elementary union probability with the sum in (1.1).

Lemma 5.4.

For every n≥1n\geq 1,

0≤an​(S)−ℙ⁡(ℰn)≤C5.4​n4​q−2​n,\displaystyle 0\leq a_{n}(S)-\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{n})\leq C_{\ref{lem:elementary}}n^{4}q^{-2n},

where C5.4C_{\ref{lem:elementary}} depends only on SS.

Proof.

The row constraints have pairwise nonproportional vectors ei,ei±eje_{i},e_{i}\pm e_{j} (i<ji<j). Two distinct row constraints therefore have rank 2​n2n on the entry array, as do two column constraints. One row constraint aa and one column constraint bb have rank 2​n−12n-1, since (span⁡(a)⊗ℝn)∩(ℝn⊗span⁡(b))=span⁡(a⊗b)(\operatorname{span}(a)\otimes\mathbb{R}^{n})\cap(\mathbb{R}^{n}\otimes\operatorname{span}(b))=\operatorname{span}(a\otimes b). By (3.3) with F=SF=S, a system of rank hh holds for at most qn2−hq^{n^{2}-h} of the qn2q^{n^{2}} entry arrays. Each pairwise intersection thus has probability at most q1−2​nq^{1-2n}. There are O⁡(n4)O(n^{4}) pairs, and the individual probabilities sum to an​(S)a_{n}(S). The union bound and the first Bonferroni lower bound give the result, also when n=1n=1 and a row and column event coincide. ∎

Statement on AI use. The authors used ChatGPT with the GPT-6 Astra model in the work described below. Before this use, the authors developed a Fourier argument based on a moment of fixed order and a precursor of the present set V⁡(θ)V(\theta). This argument estimated the contribution of approximate relations directly and already gave an improvement of the form 2−n​exp⁡(o⁡(nlog⁡n))2^{-n}\exp(o(\sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}})) for random sign matrices.

Seeking a sharp asymptotic, the authors considered arithmetic and geometric ways to control the possible relation sets and their associated frequency regions, and asked ChatGPT to explore these directions. In the ensuing discussions, the authors and ChatGPT jointly developed the classification by dimension and density, the use of a moment order that grows with nn, and separate estimates for bounded and large density loss. This method, including the weighted covering for large loss in the proof of Proposition 4.6, yielded the sharp Bernoulli asymptotic.

The authors then asked whether the argument could be extended to arbitrary finite real supports. ChatGPT proposed the approach that removes the algebraicity restriction. This extension is explained in Section 2.2 and carried out through the estimates of Section 3 and their use in Section 4, particularly Lemma 4.8 and the proof of Proposition 4.6. The authors checked, organized, and rewrote the final proofs, used ChatGPT for language editing, and take full responsibility for the paper.

Appendix A Determinant bounds for algebraic supports

The change of variables for far frequencies depends on a lower bound for a determinant with entries in a fixed finite set. When that set is algebraic, a field norm supplies a bound uniform in the dimension. We isolate this arithmetic input and compare it with the geometric estimate (4.10) used in the general proof.

Lemma A.1.

For every fixed finite set FF of real algebraic numbers there is CA.1>0C_{\ref{lem:fieldnorm}}>0 depending only on FF such that every invertible m×mm\times m matrix BB with entries in FF satisfies

|detB|≥exp⁡{−CA.1​m​log⁡(m+1)}(m≥1).\displaystyle|\det B|\geq\exp\{-C_{\ref{lem:fieldnorm}}m\log(m+1)\}\qquad(m\geq 1).
Proof.

The field K=ℚ⁡(F)K=\mathbb{Q}(F) is a number field of degree ee. Choose a positive integer HH such that H​aHa is an algebraic integer for every a∈Fa\in F. Then α=Hm​detB\alpha=H^{m}\det B is a nonzero algebraic integer in KK. Its field norm is a nonzero integer, so

1≤|NK/ℚ(α)|=∏σ:K↪ℂ|σ(α)|.\displaystyle 1\leq|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)|=\prod_{\sigma:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}}|\sigma(\alpha)|.

Set B0=max(1,|σ(a)|:a∈F,σ:K↪ℂ)B_{0}=\max(1,|\sigma(a)|:a\in F,\ \sigma:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}). For each embedding, Hadamard’s inequality gives

|σ⁡(α)|=|det(H​σ​(B))|≤(H​B0​m)m.\displaystyle|\sigma(\alpha)|=|\det(H\sigma(B))|\leq(HB_{0}\sqrt{m})^{m}.

Separate the identity embedding in the norm product. It follows that

|detB|=H−m​|α|≥H−m​(H​B0​m)−m⁡(e−1).\displaystyle|\det B|=H^{-m}|\alpha|\geq H^{-m}(HB_{0}\sqrt{m})^{-m(e-1)}.

Taking logarithms proves the result, with a constant depending only on FF and with m=1m=1 covered by the same choice. ∎

Suppose now that EE is algebraic. Translating by an element of EE preserves this property, so retain 0∈E0\in E as in the proof of Theorem 4.2. For the relation set V={v∈Ek:|⟨v,θ⟩|≤R/N}V=\{v\in E^{k}:|\langle v,\theta\rangle|\leq R/N\} used to estimate (4.4), take U=span⁡VU=\operatorname{span}V, and write r=dimUr=\dim U and d=k−rd=k-r. Because all constant configurations lie in VV, there is a basis (a~​𝟏k,v2,…,vr)(\tilde{a}\mathbf{1}_{k},v_{2},\ldots,v_{r}) of UU with columns in VV, where a~∈E∖{0}\tilde{a}\in E\setminus\{0\}.

The r−1r-1 functionals ⟨vj,θ⟩\langle v_{j},\theta\rangle, 2≤j≤r2\leq j\leq r, are independent on HkH_{k}: a linear combination vanishing there is a multiple of 𝟏k\mathbf{1}_{k}, which contradicts independence of the basis. In the chart θk=−∑i<kθi\theta_{k}=-\sum_{i<k}\theta_{i}, their coefficient rows are (vj,i−vj,k)i<k(v_{j,i}-v_{j,k})_{i<k}. Complete these rows to an invertible (k−1)×(k−1)(k-1)\times(k-1) matrix DD by adjoining dd of the coordinate rows. All entries of DD belong to the fixed finite algebraic set

F=(E−E)∪{0,1,−1}.\displaystyle F=(E-E)\cup\{0,1,-1\}.

Thus the map

θ⟼(⟨v2,θ⟩,…,⟨vr,θ⟩,θj1,…,θjd)\displaystyle\theta\longmapsto(\langle v_{2},\theta\rangle,\ldots,\langle v_{r},\theta\rangle,\theta_{j_{1}},\ldots,\theta_{j_{d}})

has inverse Jacobian, for the measure defined by eliminating one coordinate on HkH_{k}, bounded by

|detD|−1≤exp⁡{C​k​log⁡(k+1)}.\displaystyle|\det D|^{-1}\leq\exp\{Ck\log(k+1)\}.

The differences in E−EE-E come from eliminating θk\theta_{k}; the adjoined coordinate rows use only 00 and 11. For r=1r=1, there are no relation rows and DD is the identity.

On the slab set |⟨vj,θ⟩|≤R/N|\langle v_{j},\theta\rangle|\leq R/N for 2≤j≤r2\leq j\leq r, the first r−1r-1 transformed variables range over [−R/N,R/N][-R/N,R/N]. Retain the Gaussian factors at the dd adjoined coordinates and bound the others by one. This Jacobian bound gives

∫θ∈Hk|⟨vj,θ⟩|≤R/N⁡(2≤j≤r)∏i=1kωn​(θi)​𝑑θ≤eC​k​log⁡(k+1)​(2​R/N)r−1​(C/n)d.\displaystyle\int_{\begin{subarray}{c}\theta\in H_{k}\\ |\langle v_{j},\theta\rangle|\leq R/N\ (2\leq j\leq r)\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\omega_{n}(\theta_{i})\,d\theta\leq e^{Ck\log(k+1)}(2R/N)^{r-1}(C/\sqrt{n})^{d}.

For k=A​n/log⁡(n+1)+O⁡(1)k=An/\log(n+1)+O(1) with fixed AA, the cost of the inverse Jacobian is exp⁡{OE​(A​n)}\exp\{O_{E}(An)\}. Algebraic bases can still be poorly conditioned; the field norm gives a quantitative bound of a size the exponential estimates can accommodate.

For arbitrary real EE, Section 4 obtains the corresponding control by selecting a dimension and frame through maximal scaled volume, counting their approximate interpolation labels, and averaging over the bases in Lemma 3.7. Only g≤C⁡(t+2)g\leq C(t+2) completion directions then contribute the small scale η\eta, giving (4.10). The arithmetic calculation above controls this change of variables for an exact basis. Counting the possible relation configurations and their bases is a separate part of the Fourier estimate; the full small ball proof is the one given in the main text.
